repos.name: freshcart-backend
repos.tagline: Twelve .NET 10 microservices, each in a different architecture, with race conditions proven by tests
repos.problem_solved: Distributed-systems correctness claims on a CV are unfalsifiable. This repo makes them checkable: every hard guarantee (exactly-once projection, no oversubscribed capacity, gap-free invoice numbers, no duplicate outbox publishes) is implemented in production code and pinned by an N-way concurrent test against a real database engine in a Testcontainer.
repos.what_it_does: A .NET 10 / Aspire reference e-commerce backend of twelve bounded contexts behind a YARP gateway, each context deliberately built in a different architectural style (Clean, Vertical Slice + Carter/MediatR, Hexagonal, 3-tier + Dapper, event-sourced, pipes-and-filters, CQRS read model) over a different store (SQL Server, PostgreSQL/Marten, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, SQLite). Services talk asynchronously over MassTransit/RabbitMQ with transactional outboxes and synchronously over gRPC; a MassTransit state machine orchestrates the checkout saga across stock reservation, payment capture and confirmation. The gateway is a BFF: browsers hold an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie, services only ever see a short-lived minted JWT. The Angular storefront lives in a separate repo (amasen02/freshcart-web); this one is the backend, plus Bicep IaC, Helm charts and per-service CI.
repos.architecture: src/ is one solution with four groups: BuildingBlocks (CQRS abstractions, MediatR behaviors, RFC 7807 exception handler, outbox + integration-event contracts, ServiceDefaults, security middleware), Services/ (twelve contexts, most split Api/Application/Domain/Infrastructure, some deliberately flatter — Inventory and Notification are single-project, Pricing is gRPC-only), ApiGateways/FreshCart.Gateway.Yarp, and AspireAppHost. Async integration flows through MassTransit over RabbitMQ; each writer stages events in its own store's outbox (EF Core on SQL Server, Marten on Postgres, Mongo transactions in Delivery/Payment) and a background OutboxPublisher drains them. Consumers are idempotent via an inbox table. deploy/ carries docker-compose, Helm charts and raw k8s manifests; infra/ carries main.bicep plus 13 modules and dev/staging/prod param files.
highlights: Outbox drain is a claim-by-update with a crash-recovering lease, not a naive SELECT-unpublished. EntityFrameworkOutboxStore selects candidate ids, stamps them with a per-call ClaimId via a conditional ExecuteUpdateAsync that only matches rows still unclaimed or whose lease lapsed, then re-reads only the rows it actually won. Two publisher replicas therefore claim disjoint sets with no distributed lock, and a crashed drainer's rows return to the pool when the lease expires. The same pattern is implemented over Marten for the Postgres-backed Basket.

The payment one-payment-per-order invariant lives in the event store, not the read model. MongoPaymentEventStore builds a PARTIAL unique index on OrderId filtered to Version == 1 (the initiating event), so a second concurrent initiate for the same order fails with a duplicate-key error at the source of truth rather than in an asynchronously-projected SQL table. A compound unique (PaymentId, Version) index supplies optimistic concurrency, and the event batch plus a projection marker are inserted in one Mongo session transaction, so there is no dual write between the event store and the SQL read model.

Exactly-once read projections: WarehouseProjectionWriter writes the projection_inbox idempotency row inside the SAME MySQL transaction as the denormalised fact upserts, so an at-least-once redelivery cannot double-count additive aggregates (refund totals, customer lifetime value). Customer 'new vs returning' segmentation is decided from the prior lifetime-value row read inside that same transaction before the upsert advances it.

The gateway BFF token exchanger fails closed on a missing claim rather than degrading. CookieToJwtTokenExchanger caches the minted downstream JWT keyed on subject + the auth_time claim; if the cookie principal carries no authentication instant it throws, with an inline comment explaining that a constant fallback key would let a token minted for a prior session be replayed for a freshly re-authenticated one.

Delivery-slot booking is a single Mongo UpdateOne whose filter carries the capacity predicate (BookedCount < Capacity) and whose update is an $inc, so two schedulers racing for the last unit cannot both see ModifiedCount == 1. The same field-to-field predicate is reused for the open-slot list queries so filtering runs server-side.

Concurrency claims are pinned by real tests, not prose. InvoiceRepositoryTests fires 25 parallel allocators against a Testcontainers MySQL 8.0 and asserts the result set is exactly {1..25} — unique and gap-free — proving the ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE / LAST_INSERT_ID allocation is not a read-then-write. Equivalent concurrency suites exist for product SKU creation (Marten/Postgres), slot booking and outbox claim disjointness (MongoDB), and refresh-token rotation (SQL Server).

Deliberate architectural heterogeneity as the point of the repo: twelve contexts in twelve styles over six storage engines, with ADR-0003 justifying each store by access pattern (Marten JSONB for heterogeneous product attributes, Mongo 2dsphere for delivery geo, MySQL as a separate OLAP engine to make the ETL boundary explicit) and naming the rejected alternatives.

Supply-chain gates are real, not badges: a reusable workflow builds each service image, fails the job on any fixable HIGH/CRITICAL Trivy finding (exit-code 1, ignore-unfixed), and on master pushes to GHCR and keylessly signs the digest with Cosign under Sigstore OIDC with no stored signing key. Directory.Build.props promotes NuGet audit findings to build errors with two documented per-package suppressions instead of a blanket demotion.

repos.name: freshcart-web
repos.tagline: Zoneless Angular 20 storefront on signal stores, cookie-only auth and SignalR realtime
repos.problem_solved: The customer-facing SPA for the FreshCart microservices platform: it has to authenticate against a .NET Identity service through a YARP gateway without ever holding a token in JavaScript, keep order status and support chat live over SignalR, and still degrade to polling when the realtime channel is unavailable.
repos.what_it_does: An Angular 20 single-page storefront (home, catalog, product detail, basket, checkout, orders, account with MFA enrolment, an Administrator/Manager reporting dashboard, and a customer support chat plus a SupportAgent console) that talks only to same-origin /api and /hubs paths on the gateway. Authentication is an HttpOnly session cookie; the app primes an anti-forgery token, echoes XSRF-TOKEN as X-XSRF-TOKEN via Angular's withXsrfConfiguration, and attaches withCredentials only to /api/ and /hubs/ URLs. Two SignalR hubs are wrapped in a small RealtimeConnection abstraction that exposes connection state as a signal; NotificationsStore starts on authentication and tears down handlers on sign-out, while SupportChatStore connects lazily on first widget open. All state is @ngrx/signals stores, and the whole app runs zoneless (provideZonelessChangeDetection).
repos.architecture: src/app is split into core/ (auth store + functional guards, two HTTP interceptors, ApiError model, a central ApiRoutes registry, injectable Clock and timing tokens, realtime layer, toast service, title strategy), shared/ (pipes, directives, dialog service, presentational components), layout/ (shell, header, footer, toast host, notification bell) and features/ (every route lazy-loaded via loadComponent/loadChildren, with canMatch guards including a roleGuard factory). Root-provided signal stores hold cross-cutting state (AuthStore, BasketStore, NotificationsStore, SupportChatStore); feature-local state uses an unprovided signalStore (ProductListState). RxJS appears only at genuinely async edges — HTTP, SignalR, debounce, polling — and is terminated with takeUntilDestroyed. Runtime is a multi-stage Docker build serving the static bundle from non-root nginx; /api and /hubs are routed by the dev proxy locally and by the ingress in Kubernetes.
stack: Angular 20 (standalone components, zoneless change detection, signals, @angular/build application builder)
ESLint 9 + typescript-eslint + angular-eslint (incl. template a11y rules)
Docker: node:22-alpine build stage -> nginx:1.27-alpine runtime
highlights: Cookie-only auth carried all the way into SignalR. SignalrConnectionFactory builds the hub with `.withUrl(hubPath, { withCredentials: true })` and deliberately wires no accessTokenFactory — the code comment says so explicitly. This is the interesting decision: the common SignalR-in-a-SPA pattern puts a bearer token in a query string (where it lands in logs and referrers) or in JS memory (where XSS can lift it); pushing the session cookie through the gateway's cookie-to-JWT exchange removes both paths, at the cost of requiring strict same-origin routing, which the repo actually pays for in proxy.conf.json, nginx.conf and the ingress note.

Realtime lifecycle transitions are serialised through a promise chain. Both NotificationsStore and SupportChatStore keep `let lifecycle: Promise<void>` and run every start/stop as `lifecycle = lifecycle.then(transition)`. A senior reviewer cares because auth state can flap (initialize -> 401 -> sign-in) and concurrent start/stop on a HubConnection is exactly how you get duplicate handlers, orphaned sockets and leaked subscriptions. The stores also explicitly `off()` every registered handler on stop rather than relying on connection teardown.

Realtime-primary, bounded-poll fallback on the order confirmation page. An effect refetches when a notification arrives for this orderId, and independently `timer(0, pollIntervalMs)` runs under `takeWhile(attemptsRemaining > 0 && !isTerminalStatus(...))` plus `takeUntilDestroyed()`. The interval and the attempt cap are InjectionTokens (OrderPollIntervalMs, OrderPollMaxAttempts), as is a Clock token — so the timing is both bounded in production and shrinkable in tests instead of being a hard-coded setInterval.

Stale-response protection in the catalog list is deliberate, not incidental. ProductListState uses `rxMethod` with `switchMap` and a comment stating the intent: a slow earlier search response can never overwrite a newer one. Search-as-you-type races are the classic bug in this screen and it is handled at the store layer rather than per-component.

A hand-written FakeHubConnection test double (src/app/core/realtime/fake-hub-connection.ts) records sent/invoked calls, counts registered handlers, and exposes simulateReconnecting/simulateReconnected/simulateClose. It makes hub reconnect and handler-leak behaviour unit-testable with no server; the single `as unknown as HubConnection` cast is confined to one method and carries a justifying comment.

Typed error surface: ApiError.fromUnknown parses RFC7807 ProblemDetails (title, detail, traceId, validationErrors) defensively, and shared/forms/server-validation.ts maps server field errors back onto FormGroup controls case-insensitively — so backend validation reaches the right input rather than a generic toast.

Interceptor nuance: apiErrorInterceptor retries GETs once, but only on 503 (retryAfterServiceUnavailable rethrows anything else), and it exempts the sign-in/sign-up paths from the 401 session-expired handler so an anonymous failed login doesn't bounce the user off the form they are standing on.

Production hardening is real, not just claimed: non-root `USER nginx` with pre-created writable paths and a HEALTHCHECK; nginx sends CSP, X-Frame-Options DENY, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP and CORP, caches fingerprinted assets `immutable` for a year and marks index.html no-store, and logs JSON.

The CI badge overstates the state: both master CI runs concluded failure. To be precise, the Lint/Test/Build job passed every step; the 'Container · Scan · Push' job failed at 'Set up job', so the Trivy scan never ran and no image has ever been pushed to GHCR — the README's 'scanned container image on every change' is aspirational. The app cannot be run or evaluated standalone: it requires the backend gateway on https://localhost:7100 and there is no mock server, MSW layer or fixture set in the repo. The gh-pages branch is a generated static project page (sitewright, https://amasen02.github.io/freshcart-web/), not a live deployment of the SPA, and no homepage URL is set on the repo. repos.name: dupesweep
repos.tagline: Duplicate-file CLI: size → 64KB-hash → full-SHA256 funnel with reversible quarantine and restore
repos.problem_solved: Finding and reclaiming space from byte-identical duplicate files across directories without either the false positives of size-only matching or the cost of hashing every file up front — and without the data-loss risk that makes people distrust dedupe tools.
repos.what_it_does: `dsweep` walks one or more directory roots and reports groups of byte-identical files, ordered by reclaimable bytes. Detection is a three-stage funnel implemented in DuplicateFinder.cs: group by file length, then a SHA-256 of the first 64 KB, then a full-file SHA-256 on only the survivors, with stages 2 and 3 run through Parallel.ForEachAsync at a configurable degree of parallelism. Output is either a text report or JSON. Acting on the results is opt-in: `--apply quarantine` moves duplicates into a quarantine folder and writes a manifest.json of original→quarantine paths so `dsweep restore` can undo the whole operation, while `--apply delete` is the permanent alternative. Which copy survives is chosen by `--keep first|oldest|newest|shortest-path`.
repos.architecture: Single console project (src/DupeSweep, assembly `dsweep`) of 13 small single-responsibility files plus a parallel xUnit test project. Program.cs is pure orchestration (parse → scan → find → report → apply); every stage is a separate static class or small sealed type with no shared mutable state: CommandLine (hand-rolled argv parser, no dependency on System.CommandLine), FileScanner (manual recursive walk), Hashing (two-tier), DuplicateFinder (the funnel, the only stateful class, taking ScanOptions via a primary constructor), KeepSelector, QuarantineService, RestoreService, ReportWriter. Domain types in Models.cs are all sealed records (FileEntry, DuplicateGroup, DuplicateResolution, ManifestEntry, RestoreSummary), which is what makes the services testable in isolation — most tests construct records directly and never touch the CLI.
highlights: The parallel hash pass writes results into a pre-allocated `string?[]` indexed by position rather than into a ConcurrentDictionary, then groups single-threaded afterwards. Interesting because it is lock-free on the hot path *and* it preserves scan order, which is what makes `--keep first` deterministic — a concurrent-dictionary implementation would have given order-dependent results for the default keep strategy.

Destructive work is reversible by default and the reversal is tested for the dangerous case. Quarantine is a File.Move plus a JSON manifest; RestoreService refuses to move a file back if something already exists at the original path, and the test `Restore_ExistingDestination_IsSkippedWithoutOverwrite` asserts both that the recreated file is untouched *and* that the quarantined copy still exists — i.e. it pins down that the skip path loses nothing. For a tool whose worst failure mode is silent data loss, that is the right thing to have made hard to regress.

Failure is contained at file granularity, not run granularity. FileScanner catches UnauthorizedAccessException/IOException per directory and per file and keeps walking; DuplicateFinder catches the same two types per hash task into a ConcurrentBag of warnings surfaced under `-v`. The catch filters are narrow (`when (ex is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)`), so real bugs still propagate — a scan of a home directory always hits unreadable files, and throwing would waste the entire scan.
The Dockerfile runs `dotnet test` as a build stage before `dotnet publish`, so the image cannot be produced from a red tree, and the runtime stage drops to the built-in unprivileged `app` user.

Every keep strategy has an ordinal full-path tiebreaker after its primary sort key, so results are stable across filesystems with different enumeration order — a detail that is easy to omit and produces irreproducible output when omitted.

Small and young. Nine commits total (created 2026-07-02, last pushed 2026-09-04), five of which are dependabot bumps — effectively three authored commits over ~60 KB of C#. All merged PRs are dependabot; there are no external human contributions. 92 stars against that activity is disproportionate and a reviewer will notice the gap.

repos.name: fastdl
repos.tagline: Multi-connection segmented HTTP downloader CLI in .NET 10, with mirror striping and chunk resume
repos.problem_solved: Downloading large files or whole directory trees over HTTP faster than a single connection allows, and surviving interruptions without re-fetching bytes already on disk — the job commercial download managers do, as an open-source cross-platform CLI.
repos.what_it_does: `fdl` splits a file into fixed-size byte-range chunks and pulls them from a shared ConcurrentQueue with N parallel workers, writing each chunk straight to its offset in a preallocated file via RandomAccess.WriteAsync, so there is no shared file pointer and no lock. It handles single files, multi-file batches from a links file, recursive Apache/nginx autoindex folder mirrors with extension filtering, and multi-source striping where the same file is pulled across several mirror URLs. Interrupted downloads resume from a `.fdlmeta` sidecar holding a chunk bitmap, and post-processing can auto-extract downloaded zips (detected by PK magic bytes, not filename) or pack all outputs into one archive. When a server does not honour byte ranges, it falls back to a single-stream path that still handles resume, servers that silently ignore a Range header, and truncated bodies.
repos.architecture: Single executable project `src/FastDL` (AssemblyName `fdl`) with one class per concern and no DI container: Program.cs (parse -> build DownloadSpec list -> BatchDownloader -> post-process -> summarize), CommandLine.cs (hand-rolled argv switch, clamped values), HttpClientProvider.cs (one tuned SocketsHttpHandler shared by every worker), SegmentedDownloader.cs (the engine: probe, chunk-queue parallel path, single-stream fallback, per-segment retry with exponential backoff capped at 8s), BatchDownloader.cs (SemaphoreSlim-capped file-level concurrency), IndexCrawler.cs (depth-limited, root-confined autoindex crawler), ResumeStore.cs (sidecar chunk bitmap), ProgressReporter.cs (Interlocked counters plus a single 200ms background render loop with EMA speed), ZipService.cs, Format.cs, Models.cs (records: ProbeResult, DownloadSpec, DownloadResult, CrawlItem). Tests live in a parallel `tests/FastDL.Tests` project referencing the exe project directly.
highlights: Chunk-queue work distribution instead of a fixed N-way split: workers dequeue from a shared ConcurrentQueue<int>, so a fast connection naturally claims more chunks and no single slow segment holds up the finish. Worker count is min(connections, pending chunks), so small files do not spawn idle tasks.

Mirror failover is folded into the retry loop rather than bolted on: the source for each attempt is `sources[(index + workerId + attempt) % sources.Count]`, so a retry deliberately lands on a different mirror instead of hammering the one that just failed, and normal (non-retry) traffic is already striped across mirrors by chunk index.

Two correctness guards against silent range corruption that most hobby downloaders miss. The probe sends a `Range: 0-0` request and accepts segmentation only if the reply is 206 with Content-Range exactly `{HasRange: true, From: 0, To: 0}` — a server that returns 206 while ignoring the Range would otherwise produce a file that is corrupt but 'successful'. Separately, AutomaticDecompression is set to None and `Accept-Encoding: identity` is sent, with the comment that auto-decompression corrupts byte-range math.

Resume is treated as a data-integrity problem, not a convenience: the sidecar is only trusted if size, chunk size, and ETag/Last-Modified all still match the remote resource; it is written by serializing a snapshot to `.tmp` and atomically File.Move-ing over the real path so a reader never sees a half-written bitmap; and flushes are throttled to at most once per second.

The resume sidecar uses System.Text.Json source generation with an explicit comment that reflection-based serialization is disabled under single-file/AOT publish — evidence the author actually ran the published `fdl` binary rather than only `dotnet run`.

Single-stream fallback handles the awkward cases explicitly: if a resume request gets a 200 instead of 206, the partial file is deleted and the download restarts from zero with the shared progress counter re-baselined; and a body shorter than the probed size is rejected as `incomplete stream` rather than reported as success.

Progress accounting stays honest under failure: a failed chunk attempt subtracts the bytes it had already counted (`_progress.Add(-writtenThisAttempt)`) before retrying, so the percentage never overstates.

A 45-second per-read stall timeout implemented with a linked CancellationTokenSource, while HttpClient.Timeout is Infinite — an overall timeout would kill legitimate multi-hour downloads, so stall detection is pushed down to the read loop.

Zip auto-extract detects archives by the three PK signatures in the file header rather than by `.zip` extension, and resolves an extract directory that provably cannot collide with the archive file itself.

The directory crawler is confined to the crawl root by an AbsoluteUri StartsWith check, dedupes both directories and files, strips query/fragment, and explicitly skips Apache column-sort links (`?C=N;O=D`) that would otherwise cause infinite re-crawls of the same page.

Segmented and single-stream output are asserted byte-identical by SHA-256 against the source payload — a real proof that the lock-free parallel offset assembly is correct, not just that it did not crash.

repos.name: dupehunter
repos.tagline: Hardlink-aware duplicate-file finder and reclaimer CLI, TypeScript, zero runtime dependencies
repos.problem_solved: Duplicate finders that compare content alone double-count files that are already hardlinked together, overstating how much disk space a cleanup will actually free and re-reporting the same 'duplicates' after every pass. dupehunter resolves files to physical identity (device+inode) before comparing, so its reclaimable-space number matches what --delete/--hardlink really frees, and a hardlink pass is idempotent.
repos.what_it_does: A Node 20+ CLI (also usable as a library via src/index.ts) that recursively walks a directory, filters by minimum size and name-glob excludes, collapses paths that share a device+inode into a single PhysicalFile, buckets the survivors by byte size, and streaming-SHA-256-hashes only the size-collision candidates through a bounded-concurrency worker pool. It renders duplicate groups as coloured text or JSON, and can act on them: --delete removes every alias of the non-kept copies, --hardlink replaces them with links to the kept copy. Which copy survives is a --keep policy (first/oldest/newest), and --dry-run plus an interactive confirmation gate the destructive paths. Implementation is 15 small single-purpose modules under src/ with no runtime dependencies; devDependencies are only TypeScript, eslint and tsx.
stack: node:test + tsx for the test suite
GitHub Actions (CI matrix, CodeQL, OpenSSF Scorecard)
repos.architecture: Layered, one concern per file, all dependencies pointing inward. scanner.ts does the filesystem walk and returns ScannedFile records plus non-fatal WalkWarnings instead of throwing; dedupe.ts is the pure pipeline (walk -> size filter -> collapseHardlinks by device:inode -> group by size -> hash only multi-member size groups via runWithConcurrencyLimit); actions.ts turns groups into PlannedActions (plan is computed with zero filesystem writes, so --dry-run and the confirmation prompt render the exact same plan that later executes); render.ts/format.ts own all presentation including ANSI colour; cli.ts is a thin shell mapping parse -> scan -> render -> confirm -> act to three documented exit codes (0/1/2). types.ts centres the PhysicalFile abstraction — {paths[], sizeBytes, device, inode, modifiedAtMs} — which is the hinge the whole design turns on, and physical-file.ts/array-utils.ts enforce the 'a PhysicalFile always has >=1 path' invariant by throwing rather than returning undefined. index.ts re-exports the pipeline for programmatic use.
highlights: The core modelling decision: a duplicate group is a group of *physical files*, not paths. collapseHardlinks() in src/dedupe.ts keys on `${device}:${inode}` before any hashing, so an already-linked pair contributes one entry carrying two paths. Reclaimable space is then size × (physicalFiles − 1), which is provably what a cleanup frees, and re-running --hardlink finds nothing. Interesting because it is the rare case where picking the right domain type (PhysicalFile over string path) removes a whole class of accounting bugs instead of patching them; two tests in test/dedupe.test.ts assert exactly this ('reclaimable space accounts for existing hardlinks, not raw path count').

Crash-safe hardlink replacement in src/actions.ts: link(kept -> .dupehunter-<uuid>.tmp) then rename(tmp -> victim), never unlink-then-link. rename() is atomic on the same filesystem, so an interrupted or failing operation leaves the original file fully intact; the failure branch also cleans the temp file and records a per-path ActionOutcome rather than aborting the batch. Interesting because it is the one place in the tool where a naive implementation silently destroys user data, and the test 'hardlinkDuplicates: leaves the original file untouched if linking fails' pins the invariant by pointing the kept path at a nonexistent file.

Work-avoidance ordering in the pipeline: size bucketing happens first and only buckets with >=2 members are hashed (src/dedupe.ts), so unique-sized files are never read; hashing is streaming SHA-256 (src/hasher.ts) so a multi-GB file never lands in memory; and the hash fan-out is bounded by a hand-written runWithConcurrencyLimit (src/concurrency.ts) defaulting to os.availableParallelism(), which preserves input order in its results array — avoiding a dependency like p-limit and keeping the zero-runtime-dependency claim true.

Honest self-documenting limits rather than silent ones: scanner.ts's symlink handler carries a comment explaining that its visitedRealDirs guard guarantees termination but does not dedupe plain directories reached through different symlink chains — and then explains why that is safe (device+inode collapsing downstream absorbs the duplicate paths). Reviewers rarely see a repo that writes down the boundary of its own guard.

scripts/run-tests.mjs enumerates test files explicitly instead of passing a glob to `node --test`, with a comment noting that native glob support only landed in Node 22 while package.json's engines field allows Node 20. Small, but it is evidence the declared support floor is actually honoured rather than aspirational — and the CI matrix does run 20.x and 22.x on ubuntu and windows.

repos.caveats: Small and young: created 2026-07-02, 14 commits total of which only 3 are human — the entire codebase (~68KB TS) landed in the initial commit, and everything since is dependabot bumps plus one workflow addition. 23 stars, 0 forks, no external contributors, no issues/PRs from anyone but the bot. Not published to npm (README says so), so install is clone-and-npm-link. The README calls it 'fast' but there are no benchmarks anywhere in the repo, and there is no partial/head-tail hash short-circuit — every candidate in a size collision is hashed in full, so the usual optimisation of the genre is absent. Deletion is decided on size + SHA-256 equality with no byte-for-byte confirmation pass (fdupes/rdfind offer one); defensible, but it is a trust assumption a reviewer will ask about before running --delete. Duplicate groups can span filesystems, and --hardlink does not plan around that — cross-device links just fail at runtime with a per-path EXDEV outcome. `--json` is silently ignored when combined with --delete/--hardlink (cli.ts only emits JSON in the read-only path). runWithConcurrencyLimit recurses through `await runNext()`, so each worker builds a promise chain proportional to items/limit — fine at normal scale, untested at the million-file scale the README's 'ideas' section talks about. Finally, the last third of the README ('🌟 Fork, Build Upon & Extend This Project', 'we review and merge PRs within 24–48 hours', emoji bullet lists) reads as growth-hacking boilerplate bolted onto an otherwise sober, accurate document, and the OpenSSF Best Practices badge links to the generic bestpractices.dev page rather than a passing project page. The code itself is better than that section makes it sound.

repos.name: a11y-scope
repos.tagline: Self-hosted dashboard running scheduled Playwright + axe-core WCAG scans, with violation trends
repos.problem_solved: Small organisations with real ADA / EU Accessibility Act obligations (the README names school districts, nonprofits, city governments, agencies) need continuous accessibility monitoring but cannot justify commercial SaaS pricing. This packages the scan-schedule-store-alert loop into one Docker container with an embedded SQLite file, so there is no external service to pay for or operate.
repos.what_it_does: A Next.js 16 App Router application that stores a list of sites, runs headless Chromium against each one via Playwright, extracts WCAG violations with @axe-core/playwright (tag filter: wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa), and persists every failing DOM node as its own row in SQLite through Drizzle ORM. Scans are triggered three ways — a manual button, an in-process node-cron schedule per site (default `0 2 * * *`), and an unauthenticated `POST /api/webhook` intended for CI — all of which insert a `pending` scan row and return HTTP 202 while the work runs in the background. The dashboard renders overview counts, a per-site recharts trend line built from the last 30 completed scans, and a scan detail page that groups violations by axe impact (critical/serious/moderate/minor) and expands each one to show the CSS selector, the offending HTML, the axe failure summary and the deque help URL. When a completed scan's violation count meets a per-site threshold, nodemailer sends an alert; with no `SMTP_HOST` set it logs and returns instead of throwing.
highlights: Runs the cron scheduler inside the Next.js server process rather than as a separate worker: `src/instrumentation.ts` gates on `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs'` and calls `startScheduler()`, which hydrates a module-level `Map<string, cron.ScheduledTask>` from active sites; `POST /api/sites` and the webhook route then dynamically import `scheduleJob` to register newly created sites into that same live map. This is what makes the 'single container, zero external services' claim actually true — no Redis, no queue, no sidecar — and the trade-off is explicit in the code: schedules live in one process's memory, so a restart re-hydrates from the DB but multiple replicas would each fire their own copy.

The `scans` table is used as the job state machine instead of a queue. Routes insert a `pending` row, return 202 with the scan id, and hand off via `setImmediate`; `scanSite()` then transitions the row to `running`, and in a try/catch/finally writes either `done` with `completedAt`/`violationCount` or `failed` with the caught `errorMessage` persisted to the row, always closing the browser in `finally`. A reviewer gets a durable audit trail and user-visible failure reasons for free, without adding BullMQ — though nothing reaps a row left in `running` by a process crash.

Violations are stored denormalised, one row per axe node rather than per rule: `scanner.ts` loops `results.violations` then `violation.nodes`, giving each node its own id, `nodeSelector` (`node.target.join(', ')`), `nodeHtml`, and `failureSummary`, plus the wcag tags filtered out of `violation.tags` into a `wcagCriteria` string. That is why the scan detail page can sort and group purely with `count(*)` and in-memory filters, and why the trend chart is a plain `violationCount` integer per scan.

The Docker runner stage hand-copies the exact transitive dependencies the seed script needs (`bcryptjs`, `@libsql`, `libsql`, `js-base64`, `promise-limit`) into the Next.js standalone output, with a comment explaining that standalone tracing does not include `scripts/`. There is a matching commit, `fix: copy seed script deps into Docker runner stage`, so this is a diagnosed real bug rather than copied boilerplate. The stage also creates a non-root `nextjs:nodejs` (1001) user and chowns `/app/data`.

Auth is deny-by-default at the edge: `src/middleware.ts` matches everything except `_next/static`, `_next/image` and the favicon, and only lets through an explicit `PUBLIC_PATHS` allowlist (`/login`, `/api/auth`, `/api/webhook`), redirecting otherwise with a `callbackUrl` preserved. Each API route also re-checks `await auth()` independently, so the middleware is defence in depth rather than the only gate. `src/lib/auth.ts` throws at module load if `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` is unset.

repos.architecture: Single Next.js App Router process doing everything. `src/lib/` holds the seams: `schema.ts` (four Drizzle tables — users, sites, scans, violations — with inferred Select/Insert types exported), `db.ts` (a `globalThis.__db` singleton that normalises a bare path into a `file:` libSQL URL and mkdirs the parent directory), `scanner.ts` (the Playwright + axe run and DB writes), `scheduler.ts` (the in-memory cron task map), `auth.ts` (NextAuth v5 credentials + JWT sessions), `email.ts` (nodemailer alerts). repos.caveats: Small and young, and honest scale matters here: 1 star, 0 forks, created 2026-07-18, and 17 total commits of which 10 are dependabot bumps — roughly seven human commits, all by the owner. Test coverage is thin and shallow: 5 test cases across 2 files, covering schema round-trips and the SMTP-not-configured branch. The scanner, the scheduler, NextAuth wiring and every API route are untested, and `schema.test.ts` hand-writes its own CREATE TABLE DDL rather than running the Drizzle migration, so it validates that hand-written SQL, not the real schema. There are no migrations at all (`drizzle-kit push` only), no benchmarks, and no ADRs. Two documentation claims do not survive a read of the code: the README's 'implement the `ScanEngine` interface in src/lib/scanner.ts' — grep finds no `ScanEngine` anywhere; scanner.ts is one hardcoded function — and `CLAUDE.md`, which asserts Pa11y integration, PostgreSQL compatibility, visual violation heatmaps and Next.js 15, none of which match package.json or the file tree. `.github/workflows/codex-ci-triage.yml` is named 'OpenAI Codex Automated OSS Triage' but its triage step is an `echo` plus two comment lines; it makes no API call. The README's closing 'Fork, Build Upon & Extend' section (emoji headings, 'we review and merge PRs within 24-48 hours', 'we' for a solo project) reads as promotional generated boilerplate and is at odds with the ~14 dependabot PRs currently sitting open and unmerged. Security-wise the code is mostly careful — bcrypt, deny-by-default middleware, a module-load assert on `NEXTAUTH_SECRET`, a prominent README warning — but `/api/webhook` is deliberately unauthenticated and will, for any URL posted to it, create a permanent site row AND register a recurring daily cron job that launches a browser against that URL: no shared secret, no rate limit, no host allowlist, unbounded growth, and an outbound-request primitive pointed at whatever the caller names. `docker-compose.yml` also hardcodes `NEXTAUTH_SECRET=change-me-in-production` inline, which contradicts the README's own warning, and `scripts/seed-user.mjs` seeds `admin@example.com / admin123`. Functionally the scope is narrower than 'monitoring' suggests: each scan hits exactly one URL, there is no crawler or sitemap traversal, and the README's '57% of WCAG issues' figure is an axe-core claim carried over, not something this repo measures.

repos.name: diagif
repos.tagline: CLI agent that turns a topic into a fact-grounded, browser-inspected, gate-verified looping GIF
repos.problem_solved: Turning a technical topic into an explanatory animated diagram normally means either hand-authoring it in a design tool or letting an LLM invent both the content and the layout. diagif automates the pipeline while refusing to let the model assert anything that is not traceable to a fetched source, and refusing to deliver a GIF that has not been mechanically verified frame by frame.
repos.what_it_does: A Node CLI (`diagif make "<topic>"`) that runs a multi-stage agent: collect research from HN/GitHub/public pages (optionally Brave/Exa/Tavily/Reddit), have a model produce a fact sheet whose every quote must be found verbatim in the fetched extract, produce a brief, then propose a JSON "scene" that is schema-validated, deterministically repaired, and measured inside real Chromium before rendering. The renderer captures frames headlessly, encodes a looping GIF (Pillow guaranteed, gifski/gifsicle optional), and a Python quality gate decodes the result and checks frame delays, loop-seam hashes, static-region flicker and reserved colours before promotion. Every model call is budgeted and durably accounted, and every step is content-hash keyed so a run can be resumed. It also drafts a LinkedIn post but never publishes anything.
stack: OpenAI + Anthropic HTTP APIs; codex-cli / claude-cli subprocess adapters
repos.architecture: Layered, port-and-adapter. `src/agent/harness.js` (25 KB) is the pipeline driver: 00-budget-probe/00-scout, 01-research, 02-brief, 03-scene-aN, 04-render-aN, 05-critic-aN, with every dependency injected through `defaultDependencies()` so tests substitute ports rather than loading the renderer. Underneath sit independent subsystems: `src/agent/research/*` (provider adapters, SSRF-hardened fetcher, HTML extraction, 7-day cache), `src/agent/brains/*` (mock, openai, anthropic, codex-cli, claude-cli behind one `complete()` contract with JSON-envelope extraction, truncation/refusal handling and retry), `src/agent/claims.js` + `scene-repair.js` + `scene-inspect.js` (grounding ledger, deterministic repair, Chromium geometry measurement), `src/renderer/*` (UMD modules loaded in a manifest-fixed order into a self-contained page.html with no network access), `src/capture` + `src/encode` (frame capture, encoder ladder), and `src/quality/verify.py` (artifact-level GIF verification). `src/agent/run-store.js` persists a schema-validated `run.json` plus per-step evidence under `out/<slug>/`.
highlights: Grounding is enforced mechanically, not by prompt. `validateFactSheet` requires 6-12 facts, and each quote must survive NFKC + punctuation + whitespace normalisation and then be found as a substring of the actual fetched extract (min 12 chars / 4 words); it records the match offset and a SHA-256 of the extract. A fact sheet whose source metadata differs from what the collector actually retrieved is rejected outright.

A claim-coverage ledger (`src/agent/claims.js`) enumerates every text slot the diagram will render (title, node labels, edge labels, annotation rows, mindmap branches) and requires each to be covered by a claim citing either a fact ID or the literal token `authoring`. A slot classifier auto-approves purely connective text but escalates anything containing numbers, percentages, `Nx`, comparatives, or absolutes like `only/always/guarantees` - so quantitative claims cannot slip in as decoration.

Layout defects are found by measuring the real render, not by asking the model. `scene-inspect.js` opens the scene in Chromium and uses `getBBox()` to detect labels exceeding two lines, labels violating a 4 px inset, node-node overlap, annotation-annotation and annotation-node collisions, unloaded fonts, and an edge path-geometry self-check with a 0.5% relative-error tolerance. Errors feed `deterministicRepair()`, which fixes them mechanically (with an edit trace) so a layout problem does not cost a model call.

The model-call budget is treated as durable state: `createBrainRunner` increments `run.budget.modelCallsUsed` and persists the run *before* dispatching the request, so a crashed or killed process cannot silently reset the budget. Scout runs additionally carry an aggregate budget across all child runs.

Resume is content-addressed rather than timestamp-based. Each step's reuse key hashes its inputs together with the JSON Schema, the prompt version, resource hashes, and a browser identity that includes a SHA-256 of the Chromium executable - so upgrading Playwright or changing the brand invalidates exactly the downstream steps and nothing more.

`src/quality/verify.py` verifies the delivered artifact, not the intent: it decodes the GIF and checks the frame-delay grid, that delays sum to the declared duration, a <=250 decoded-frame cap, loop-seam equality by SHA-256 of `seam.png` against `frame_0000.png`, static-region flicker via a min-filtered difference mask, and exact reserved-colour pixel counts - then emits a 3x3 contact sheet for human review.

The page fetcher is SSRF-hardened well beyond the usual URL blocklist: it rejects credentials in URLs, rejects private IPv4 ranges plus IPv6 ULA/link-local/multicast/6to4/Teredo/NAT64 and IPv4-mapped forms, resolves DNS itself and then *pins the resolved address into the request's `lookup` callback* so a rebind between check and connect cannot occur, re-validates on each of up to 3 redirects, forbids non-identity content-encoding, and caps both raw (2 MB) and decoded (1 MB) bytes.

Deliberate epistemic honesty in the product surface: scout scores are labelled `heuristic virality` and documented as an ordering aid; a critic running without vision records `readability` and `hook` as `unmeasured` rather than `pass`, and the README states that `delivered-with-warnings` is not a claim of visual review.

`scripts/sanitize-public-docs.js` scans git-tracked files for secret and private-path signatures (API-key prefixes, private-key headers, `C:\Users\`, `/home/<user>/`, internal hostnames) and deliberately assembles its own signature literals from string fragments so the scanner can scan itself without self-matching. It runs as a required CI step.

Rendering is offline-by-construction: `docs/CONTRACT.md` freezes a UMD module contract with a fixed load order, and the capture page has exactly two injection points for data-URI fonts and inlined runtime scripts - no `<script src>`, no `fetch`, no `url(file:)` anywhere in the rendered page.

repos.name: postwright
repos.tagline: Node CLI that drafts X, LinkedIn and dev.to posts and won't publish without readback proof
repos.problem_solved: Publishing to real social accounts from a script is a non-idempotent, irreversible side effect that most tooling treats as a pass/fail HTTP call — so a retry after an ambiguous outcome duplicate-posts. postwright stages every draft on local disk, gates it behind twelve named rules, and makes 'published' mean 'found again on the live profile', not 'the click returned'.
repos.what_it_does: A zero-dependency Node 24 CommonJS CLI (`draft`, `lint`, `status`, `release`, `run`, `auth`, `doctor`) that stages one topic into local X, LinkedIn and dev.to files plus a manifest, lints them against twelve rules (R1-R12) in `src/core/lint.js`, and only publishes one channel at a time behind an explicit `--confirm`. dev.to goes through the Forem REST API (POST with `published:false`, then a separate GET to read the article back); X and LinkedIn go through Python CDP drivers (`src/publish/x_publish.py`, `linkedin_publish.py`) executed by an external `browser-harness` binary against the operator's already-logged-in browser. Draft text comes either from a deterministic template (explicitly marked as filler) or from a Claude CLI subprocess called with a JSON schema. An optional animated GIF is rendered by a sibling `diagif` tool and its bytes are SHA-256-pinned into the manifest, with a Pillow subprocess measuring how much of a mind-map frame is empty.
stack: CommonJS (no build step, zero runtime dependencies)
Chrome DevTools Protocol (via an external browser-harness binary)
highlights: Release has three outcomes, not two: released, refused, and uncertain. The browser drivers tag their failure with a `stage`, and only `stage == "readback"` (post-click, irreversible) is surfaced as uncertain; `release()` turns any publisher throw into 'Release outcome is uncertain; verify manually before any retry' and deliberately leaves the on-disk `inflight` receipt in place so a retry is blocked. `run` stops the channel sequence at the first refusal or uncertainty instead of continuing. This is the right model for a non-idempotent action and is where most publishing scripts duplicate-post.

Success is defined by readback, on both transports. `verifyReadback` in `src/commands/release.js` compares the returned owner plus the exact text/title against what was sent; `publishDevto` returns `readBack.title`/`readBack.body_markdown` from a follow-up GET rather than echoing the request; the X and LinkedIn drivers re-navigate to the profile timeline and match normalised post text. Pre-publish, they also assert the composed editor text equals the intended text, assert the session's handle/profile is the expected account, and (LinkedIn) assert the audience is public before clicking.

A content-hash interlock between lint and release. `payloadHash` in `src/core/store.js` hashes the channel file plus `first-comment.md` plus `asset.gif` with NUL separators and throws on symlinks; `release` refuses if the manifest's recorded hash no longer matches. You cannot lint a clean draft and then swap the file before publishing — a gap that a 'lint then post' pipeline normally leaves wide open.

The rule *messages* are decoupled from the rules (`src/core/evidence.js`) specifically so the operator's private account analytics stay out of a public repo: shipped defaults state the direction of each finding qualitatively, and real figures load from a gitignored `postwright.evidence.json`. An explicit, documented publish-safety boundary — and, ironically, the exact reason the shipped test suite is red (see caveats).

R12 plus `assertSafeTopic` scan every publishable file for absolute Windows paths, email addresses, private-key markers, bearer tokens, credential-shaped strings, and the machine's own `os.hostname()` / `os.userInfo().username` before a release is allowed — leak prevention aimed at the operator's own environment, not just at secrets.

The LinkedIn driver locates controls from a freshly fetched CDP accessibility tree by role and accessible name rather than CSS selectors, re-fetching after media attaches because the compose surface remounts, with the reasoning written into the file (LinkedIn's class names churn more than its AX roles). The X driver uses `Input.insertText` because DraftJS ignores DOM writes and `DOM.setFileInputFiles` because synthetic change events cannot carry a real file.

Subprocess hardening throughout: `shell: false` everywhere; a `.cmd`/`.bat`/`.ps1` path is refused as the Claude CLI executable (Node 24 EINVAL, and enabling the shell would make args injectable); `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`/`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` are stripped from the child env so a stale gateway variable cannot silently redirect the prompt; the browser job file is written 0600 into a mkdtemp dir and removed in a `finally`.

Errors carry a `safe` flag (`src/core/errors.js`); anything unmarked is replaced by a generic sentence before it reaches stdout, on the stated grounds that provider errors routinely echo request bodies and headers. `auth` likewise distinguishes `unauthenticated` from `unknown`, refusing to report a broken probe as a definite negative.
Thread publishing is refused outright (`posts.length !== 1`) rather than half-attempted, because a thread that fails midway leaves account state the tool cannot reconcile.
repos.architecture: Thin `bin/postwright.js` -> `src/cli.js` -> a hand-rolled `src/cli-args.js` with a per-command option grammar (arity table, no third-party parser) -> one module per command in `src/commands/`. `src/core/` holds the shared spine: `store.js` (slug validation incl. Windows device names, symlink refusal, atomic temp-file-plus-rename JSON writes, payload hashing), `lint.js` (all twelve rules in one pure-ish function returning per-rule and per-channel verdicts, where 'cross' rules gate every channel), `evidence.js`, `config.js` (config file -> env var -> platform default resolution, memoised, failing loudly on a present-but-malformed file), `errors.js`. `src/model/` separates draft generation (`brain.js` Claude CLI, `editorial.js` template/curated fallback) from the gates. `src/publish/` is the only code that can make something public, and every path into it is injectable for tests: `social.js` refuses without a caller-supplied `browserSession`, and the real session is constructed only inside a confirmed release.
engineering_signals: test/ with 90 node:test cases across 15 unit files and 2 integration files (test/unit/*.test.js, test/integration/*.test.js); each of R1-R12 has its own named test, as do the uncertain-vs-refused outcome, the inflight-reservation retention, the payload-hash interlock and the CLI grammar

Publisher tests mock `fetch` and the browser session rather than calling out; test/integration/cli-safety.test.js spawns the real binary to prove `release` without `--confirm` exits non-zero before any account interaction

Zero runtime dependencies (no `dependencies` key in package.json; nothing installs on clone)

Dense 'why' comments at the actual decision points (evidence.js, config.js, browser-session.js, release.js, brain.js, mindmap-fill.js), not restated code
repos.caveats: Brand new and unproven: created and pushed 2026-09-06, a single commit (ea50df6), 0 stars, 0 forks, no topics, no tags or releases, version 0.1.0. The only CI run to date is RED (run 34012429136), and I reproduced it: `npm test` on a clean clone gives 89/90, with test/unit/lint.test.js:61 asserting the R2 message matches /2, 7, 10 and 26 views/ — a figure that only exists in the operator's gitignored postwright.evidence.json. The shipped suite therefore cannot pass as published, which undercuts the README's 'npm test runs the full test suite offline'. The README also says the account handles 'are configuration, not something baked into the tool's premise'; they are not — the handles are hardcoded in four source files (release.js EXPECTED_OWNER, auth.js CANONICAL, lint.js OPERATOR_LINKEDIN, browser-session.js defaults) and lint's --x-evidence validator hardcodes the path `/amasen02/status/`, with no config key for any of them, so a fork must edit source. The entire X/LinkedIn path depends on an external `browser-harness` binary that is not in this repo and not referenced to any package registry, so it is unverifiable from here; the two Python drivers (508 of ~3,259 total lines) call globals that harness injects (list_tabs, js, cdp, click_at_xy) and have no tests of their own — the JS tests only mock the driver boundary. The measured-engagement claims behind R1-R12 are, by deliberate design, unaccompanied by numbers, so to an outside reader the 'evidence' is assertion rather than data. repos.name: polyai-dotnet
repos.tagline: One DI-registered C# interface over OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama and Azure OpenAI
repos.problem_solved: A .NET service that wants to talk to more than one LLM provider has to choose between Semantic Kernel (a large orchestration framework) and Microsoft.Extensions.AI (interfaces with no implementations), then hand-write the HTTP, SSE parsing, tool-schema and error handling for each provider. This library is the small middle layer: five provider implementations behind one interface, registered into the ASP.NET Core DI container with a fluent builder.
repos.what_it_does: PolyAI.DotNet is a ~1,800-line C# library (net9.0) exposing IPolyAIClient with three operations — ChatAsync, StreamAsync (IAsyncEnumerable<string> over SSE) and StructuredAsync<T> — implemented for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Ollama and Azure OpenAI. Providers are registered through services.AddPolyAI(o => o.UseOpenAI(...).UseAnthropic(...)), each getting its own named IHttpClientFactory client, and an IPolyAIRouter resolves a provider by name with a configured default. Tool/function calling is driven by [PolyAITool]/[PolyAIParam] attributes: ToolRegistry reflects over an object, maps CLR parameter types to JSON Schema nodes, and ToolSchemaWriter renders the one schema object that OpenAI (function.parameters), Anthropic (input_schema) and Gemini (parameters) each wrap differently. All failures derive from PolyAIException, with ProviderAuthException (401/403), ProviderRateLimitException (429, carrying RetryAfter) and ProviderException (status code plus raw body) as the concrete types.
repos.architecture: src/PolyAI is split into Abstractions (IPolyAIClient, IPolyAIRouter, ChatMessage/ChatOptions/ChatResponse/TokenUsage/ToolCall), Providers (one folder per provider, all deriving from an internal abstract ProviderBase), Tools (attributes, JsonSchemaNode, ToolRegistry, ToolSchemaWriter), Errors, and Extensions (ServiceCollectionExtensions + PolyAIBuilder + PolyAIRouter). ProviderBase holds the shared behaviour that must not diverge per provider: the malformed-response boundary, EnsureSuccessAsync status-to-exception mapping, the SSE line reader, and the prompt-based StructuredAsync<T>. Provider classes are internal and sealed; only the abstractions, the attributes and the builder are public. AzureOpenAIProvider is composition rather than duplication — it constructs an OpenAIProvider with a rewritten BaseUrl and lets a DelegatingHandler on the named HttpClient swap Bearer auth for the api-key header. Tests live in tests/PolyAI.Tests with a Fakes/ FakeHttpMessageHandler and a separate QaProbes/ suite (P1-P6) of adversarial probes.
highlights: A single malformed-response boundary in ProviderBase.ReadChatResponseAsync takes the per-provider parse function as a delegate and runs it *inside* the try, so every payload failure becomes a ProviderException carrying Provider, StatusCode and the raw ResponseBody with the parse error as InnerException. Interesting because it converts the documented invariant 'every failure of this SDK is a PolyAIException' from a README claim into something structurally enforced — and the catch filter is deliberately narrowed to exactly JsonException, InvalidOperationException and ArgumentOutOfRangeException, with a comment stating that anything else is an SDK defect and must keep escaping rather than being swallowed. MalformedResponseTests then drives 4 providers x 3 payload shapes (truncated JSON, empty 200, the literal `null`) through it.

The SSE reader is written as `while(true) { ReadLineAsync(cancellationToken) }` and never uses StreamReader.EndOfStream, with an in-code explanation: EndOfStream refills the buffer with a synchronous, non-cancellable read, so on an open-but-idle connection the loop condition parks and the CancellationToken is never observed. Interesting because it is a genuinely non-obvious cancellation bug that only bites on long-lived LLM streams, and it was found and fixed as its own commit (a8d0513, 'honour cancellation in provider streaming loops') rather than being designed in.

Tool schema generation is fail-fast and cross-provider-constrained. An unmapped parameter type does not fall back to "string" — ToolRegistry throws PolyAIException at discovery time naming the tool and the parameter, with the rationale that a silently mislabelled schema surfaces much later as an unexplained binding failure. Separately, `date-time` is the only JSON Schema `format` ever emitted, because Gemini rejects other string formats ('only enum and date-time are supported for STRING type'), so Guid/DateOnly/TimeOnly are described as plain strings. Interesting because it is lowest-common-denominator reasoning across five wire formats, written down in the code rather than discovered by users. Recursion into nested collections is also bounded at depth 8 specifically to avoid an uncatchable StackOverflowException on a self-referential IEnumerable<T>.

Azure OpenAI is implemented by composition: AzureOpenAIProvider validates endpoint/deployment, builds `{endpoint}/openai/deployments/{name}` and delegates every call to an inner OpenAIProvider, while the Azure-specific auth (api-key header instead of Bearer, api-version query parameter) lives in an AzureAuthHandler DelegatingHandler attached to the named IHttpClientFactory client. Interesting because the handler is attached to the factory registration rather than to a hand-constructed HttpClient, which is what keeps consumer-added handlers (logging, Polly, tracing) in the request pipeline — and that was itself a bug fixed in commit 0bf0d41.

PolyAIBuilder.Build() rejects an unusable configuration at AddPolyAI time — no providers registered, or WithDefaultProvider naming a provider that was never registered — with the reasoning that the alternative is a container that builds clean, passes health checks, and then throws on the first user request. The Azure options are deliberately held until Build() so a rejected call does not leave a half-populated service collection.

The repo ships an adversarial QA probe suite (QaProbes/P1-P6) that encodes known defects as Skip-attributed tests with a written explanation of the failure mode, instead of deleting or hiding them — e.g. P2 documents that StreamAsync never disposes its HttpResponseMessage, P3 that StructuredAsync applies a snake_case naming policy to the caller's own type. Interesting as a practice, though see caveats: several of these skips are now stale or contradict the shipped behaviour.

(1) The NuGet package is not published. https://www.nuget.org/packages/PolyAI.DotNet returns 404 and the nuget.org search index returns 0 hits for it, so the README's NuGet version badge, the repo's homepage link and the `dotnet add package PolyAI.DotNet` quickstart all fail today; the CI publish job is gated on a `chore(release)` commit-message prefix that has never been used in the repo's 30 commits. (2) The GitHub v1.0.0 release is titled 'Universal .NET LLM & Vector Client' and its notes claim 'built-in retry and rate limiting resilience' and '.NET 8+', none of which match the code — there is no vector or embedding surface anywhere in src/, there is no retry or backoff policy (only a RetryAfter value surfaced on an exception for the caller to honour), and the csproj targets net9.0 only. On tests: I could not run `dotnet test` (no .NET SDK on this machine), so the README's '135 xUnit tests' is unverified; my attribute count is 119 [Fact] + 5 [Theory] (~139 cases), and 22 of those cases carry Skip attributes referencing an internal 'GRO-...' tracker that is not public, which the README does not mention. At least one skip is stale — P4_2_FromInstance_scans_the_runtime_type_of_the_instance is still skipped although commit 77b9329 fixed exactly that defect — and P4_4 asserts a complex parameter should map to schema type "object", which the current implementation deliberately rejects with an exception instead, so that probe would now fail rather than pass if re-enabled. A documented defect is still open in shipped code: StreamAsync does not dispose its HttpResponseMessage (confirmed by reading GeminiProvider.StreamAsync), and the probes for it are skipped rather than fixed. StructuredAsync<T> is prompt-based, not schema-enforced: it appends a 'reply with JSON' user message, strips markdown fences with string matching, and deserializes using JsonNamingPolicy.SnakeCaseLower against the caller's own type — the repo's own P3 probes flag that naming-policy behaviour as a defect and skip them, so 'typed structured output' is weaker than the README implies. Ollama tool calling is genuinely absent (the README's table is honest about that). Reach is zero: 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, 0 open issues, no external contributors — every non-Dependabot commit is the author's. The README's closing promotional section (emoji headings, 'we review and merge PRs within 24-48 hours', an ideas backlog) reads as marketing on a project with no contributors, and the README's '~20 kB package' and the Semantic Kernel size comparison are unverifiable from the repo. README and SECURITY.md also disagree on the vulnerability acknowledgement SLA (48 hours vs 72 hours). Finally, it is small: 1,811 lines of source, 4,623 lines including tests — the quality is in the reasoning and the error contract, not in scale.

repos.name: credscan
repos.tagline: Python CLI that scans source, the git index, and .claude/.cursor/MCP configs for secrets
repos.problem_solved: Generic secret scanners look at source code, but AI coding agents keep plaintext API keys in JSON config files (.claude/settings.json, .cursor/mcp.json, mcp.json) and in local session/shell-history logs, where a line-oriented `KEY=value` regex misses them once the key is JSON-quoted.
repos.what_it_does: credscan is a dependency-free Python CLI (`credscan scan [path]`) that walks a directory, or the git index with `--staged`, and reports likely-leaked credentials with the matched value redacted before it is ever printed. It ships ten rules: shape regexes for AWS access key IDs and secret keys, PEM private keys, JWTs, GitHub token prefixes and Bearer headers; a whole-file rule for GCP service-account JSON; a generic `api_key = ...` assignment rule; a Shannon-entropy fallback at 4.5 bits/char over tokens of 20+ characters; and `mcp-config-secret`, which actually parses `mcpServers` JSON and walks `env`/`headers`/`args` for literal secrets. `--agent-artifacts` narrows a scan to just the AI-agent paths, `--json` emits machine-readable output, and exit code 1 on findings makes it a CI gate. Suppression is via a `.credscanignore` glob file or an inline `credscan:ignore` marker, both deliberately visible in a diff.
stack: Python 3.10+ (standard library only — pyproject declares no runtime dependencies)
argparse CLI with a `credscan` console-script entry point
Multi-stage Dockerfile on python:3.14-slim, non-root runtime user
GitHub Actions: CI matrix, CodeQL, OpenSSF Scorecard, Dependabot
repos.architecture: src/ layout with one module per concern and no cross-tier coupling: cli.py maps argv to an exit code; scanner.py walks the tree (or the git index) and orchestrates the rule tiers; detectors.py holds `LineRule`/`ContentRule` dataclasses plus the entropy fallback; agent_artifacts.py holds the path predicate and the structural `McpConfigSecretRule`; entropy.py, allowlist.py, redact.py, render.py and git_integration.py are each ~15-60 lines with a single job; models.py defines the frozen `Finding`/`Severity` types. tests/ mirrors src/ one module per module, plus end-to-end CLI tests.
highlights: Three-tier rule precedence with character-span claiming in `scanner.scan_text`: structural content rules run first, then shape-specific line rules, then the generic entropy fallback, and each tier skips any span an earlier tier already claimed. The dedup key is span *overlap*, not matched text — a JWT's dots split the entropy rule's candidate-token regex, so a text-equality check would let a fragment of an already-classified secret be re-reported under a second rule ID. CHANGELOG.md records this as an observed bug (a GitHub token in an MCP config firing both `github-token` and `mcp-config-secret`), not a hypothetical.

`--staged` reads the git *index blob* (`git show :<path>`), not the working-tree copy, and tests/test_git_integration.py proves it by rewriting the file after `git add` and asserting the staged secret is still reported. A pre-commit gate that reads the working tree can be fooled by exactly that sequence.

`mcp-config-secret` parses the config as JSON and recursively descends `mcpServers`, harvesting strings only from `env`/`headers` dicts and `args` lists, then filtering `${VAR}`/`$VAR` placeholders. The placeholder filter is the load-bearing part: a correctly-written MCP config is mostly `${...}`, so without it the rule would be pure false positives. The value-shape check is factored out of detectors.py as `matches_known_secret_shape()` so a bare value with no `key = ` context can be tested against the same shape rules.

Redaction is structural, not procedural: `scanner._finding()` calls `redact()` when constructing the `Finding`, and the frozen dataclass has only a `redacted_match` field — there is no place for a raw secret to live, so no renderer or JSON path can leak one by accident.

The `github-token` rule exists because of a measured blind spot, documented in CHANGELOG: GitHub's near-hex token alphabet routinely falls *under* the 4.5 bits/char entropy threshold, so the generic detector silently missed one of the most common credential types until a dedicated shape rule was added.

The Dockerfile's builder stage runs `ruff check . && pytest -q` as part of `docker build`, so the image cannot be produced from a red tree; the runtime stage reinstalls from the tested source and drops to uid 1000.
engineering_signals: tests/ with 9 modules and ~82 test functions (21 detectors, 15 agent-artifacts, 11 CLI, 10 scanner, 6 allowlist, 5 entropy, 5 git-integration, 5 render, 4 redact)

repos.name: memory-mismatch-lab
repos.tagline: SQLite agent-memory adapter with tenant scoping, correction lineage, and byte-exact context packing
repos.problem_solved: Agent memory layers return answers that look plausible but silently cross tenant boundaries, ignore corrections, resurrect deleted facts through summaries, or blow a context budget. There is usually no way to prove which of those happened.
repos.what_it_does: Implements a provenance-preserving memory adapter over SQLite where every operation (add, correct, query, delete, summarise, context build, audit) is keyed on an explicit Scope of tenant_id/user_id/project_id, plus a seven-case conformance benchmark that runs the same fixtures against a deliberately naive append-only baseline. Corrections keep immutable history via corrects_id/superseded_by chains; deletion tombstones the whole lineage and redacts values and derived summary text from audit exports; conflicting active values return a `review` status rather than picking one. A Utf8ByteAccountant serialises the context packet and trims it to an exact UTF-8 byte budget. The CLI demo writes benchmark.json, an escaped standalone benchmark.html, audit.json, a context packet, and a SHA-256 receipt, all committed under artifacts/demo/.

Identity is caller-supplied entity_id + fact_key; display names are never used for resolution. Summaries track contributor fact IDs and are invalidated when any contributor stops being an active head.

Deletion tombstones the full correction lineage and redacts derived summary text, with a dedicated fixture case (deletion_no_summary_resurrection) covering resurrection through summaries

repos.name: citation-drift-lab
repos.tagline: Offline Markdown RAG that cites exact character spans, then re-audits those spans when docs change
repos.problem_solved: A stored RAG answer keeps citing a document that has since been edited. The quoted text may still exist, may have moved, may have had a number changed, or may be gone — and nothing in a normal pipeline tells you which, so a stale answer keeps looking correctly sourced.
repos.what_it_does: Ingests Markdown into versioned sources (SHA-256 of the full text, ATX heading ancestry, exact half-open Python string offsets), answers a question through a compiled LangGraph StateGraph with a bounded revise-or-abstain loop, and writes an answer receipt containing each claim's citations. A separate `audit` command replays every citation independently against a new version of the source and classifies it: unchanged, relocated (quote found at a different offset), source_missing, and material-change flags derived from comparing the numeric-literal set and negation-word presence between old and new text. Output is JSON receipts plus an html.escape'd static report. The default path is model-free and network-free; Ollama embedding and chat are opt-in.
repos.architecture: ingest.py (Markdown to versioned chunks with offsets) -> retrieval.py (deterministic BM25-like `lexical_bm25`, or `hybrid_bm25_ollama` fusing lexical and cosine ranks) -> graph.py (a real compiled StateGraph: prepare -> retrieve -> validate, then conditionally answer, revise and loop, or abstain, bounded by an explicit 0-3 counter and the graph recursion limit) -> audit.py (per-citation drift classification) -> report.py (escaped static HTML). Strict Pydantic models at every boundary reject extra fields and invalid spans.
highlights: Citations are exact half-open character offsets into the stored source text, so an audit can verify a quote by slicing the original string rather than by re-embedding or re-asking a model
Drift is classified per citation, independently of the answer, and distinguishes a relocated quote (still valid) from a materially changed one (numeric set or negation flipped)
Source integrity is enforced, not assumed: tests assert that a forged version hash and forged nested chunk metadata are both rejected

Provider handling is defensive — Ollama URLs must be credential-free loopback HTTP(S) with no query or fragment, calls are timed out, and chat failure never silently falls back to the lexical path (each asserted by a test)
Retrieval is named honestly in the code (`lexical_bm25`), and the README states outright that a surviving exact quote proves lexical integrity, not semantic entailment
engineering_signals: tests/test_public_behavior.py: 25 test functions (~16KB), including CRLF offsets not being newline-normalized, prompt-like Markdown treated as inert data, hostile fields escaped in HTML, and an ask receipt round-tripping directly into audit

repos.name: mcp-breakbench
repos.tagline: Spawns a real MCP server over stdio and turns its failures into deterministic JSON receipts
repos.problem_solved: When an agent fails on an MCP tool call, it is hard to tell whether the agent, the tool's schema, the transport, or a silent contract change is at fault. Reproducing the failure normally means re-running the agent and hoping.
repos.what_it_does: Launches a configured MCP server as a real stdio subprocess using the official Python SDK, snapshots its advertised tool contracts, and executes only the cases a local `allow_tools` allowlist permits. Each case yields a typed receipt with an explicit outcome — call timeout, protocol error, transport error, SDK output-schema rejection, client runtime error, or safe-skip-not-allowlisted — plus a drift diff against a saved baseline snapshot. Output is deterministic JSON and an escaped static HTML report. The demo ships two synthetic local servers (a fixture server and one that exits early) and reproduces invalid input, a timeout with same-session recovery, a tool-origin error, output-schema rejection, redaction, annotation-safe skipping, and tool drift.
stack: Official MCP Python SDK (mcp==2.1.1, pinned exactly)
repos.architecture: config.py validates the run spec (command, argv, explicit allowlist, cases, numeric limits) before anything is spawned; client.py opens the stdio session and paginates tool discovery under initialization and discovery deadlines; runner.py drives cases inside anyio, mapping raised exceptions — including recursing into BaseExceptionGroup — onto an Outcome enum; snapshot.py builds and diffs contract snapshots with conservative rename detection; redaction.py provides a recursive Redactor and a byte-bounded stderr capture; schemas.py validates JSON Schemas and instances; report.py emits escaped HTML.
highlights: Nothing a server advertises can authorize a call: tool descriptions and annotations are discovery data only, and an unlisted tool produces a SAFE_SKIP_NOT_ALLOWLISTED receipt (covered by test_discovery_only_never_calls_tools)
Non-local $ref, $dynamicRef and $recursiveRef in a tool schema are rejected before any tool call is made, while local fragment refs still resolve and run — both directions are tested

Failure taxonomy is explicit rather than a stack trace: distinct outcomes for call timeout, protocol error, transport error, and SDK output-schema rejection, with exception-group unwrapping so a nested cause is classified correctly
Everything is bounded — initialization, discovery time, tool pages, tool count, call time, stderr bytes, and result output — so a misbehaving server cannot hang or flood the harness
Redaction is recursive over arguments and results and preserves schema property definitions while masking values; stderr capture normalizes platform newlines and truncates at a valid Unicode boundary

repos.name: jurytrace
repos.tagline: Two LLM judges scored in parallel; every cited span checked against the source trace
repos.problem_solved: LLM-as-judge evaluation produces verdicts you cannot audit: a judge can assert a rationale that quotes text the trace never contained, and disagreement between judges is silently averaged away. JuryTrace refuses to auto-decide when the two judges disagree or when a quoted evidence span does not byte-match the original trajectory, and routes those cases to a durable human review queue.
repos.what_it_does: Reads typed JSONL trajectories (trace_id / input / output / golden_label), hashes the raw file bytes with SHA-256, and dispatches each trace to exactly two independently configured judges concurrently through a LangGraph StateGraph whose nodes are hard_gates, dispatch_judges, score_and_compare and persist_clean/persist_reviews. Each judge result is parsed against a Pydantic model with extra="forbid", and every EvidenceSpan is re-checked against the original trace: source[start:end] must equal the quoted string exactly, or the result becomes an invalid_evidence failure rather than a decision. Agreed verdicts are written to JSON, JSONL receipts and an HTML-escaped report; disagreements, timeouts, malformed output and provider errors go into a SQLite review_queue, where a human resolution is bound by foreign key to the exact (run_id, dataset_hash, trace_id) row. Ships offline deterministic fixture judges by default and an optional Ollama adapter.
repos.architecture: src/ layout package (models, providers, workflow, store, report, cli). Deterministic gates live in the graph, not in judge judgment: budget checks, asyncio.timeout deadlines, evidence validation, comparison and persistence are all workflow-owned. Providers implement one abstract Judge method that turns a trajectory into a typed proposed verdict; a configuration_key ensures the two judges are genuinely distinct. Persistence is a two-table SQLite schema (review_queue, resolutions) with CHECK constraints and a composite foreign key so a resolution cannot exist without its queued row.
highlights: Evidence spans are verified by exact slice comparison against the original trace (validate_evidence in workflow.py), so a fabricated quote becomes a hard failure instead of a decision — there is a test named test_fabricated_evidence_span_is_a_hard_failure

Every provider failure mode is typed rather than swallowed: JudgeFailure has kinds timeout, malformed_output, provider_error, invalid_evidence, and a bare-except at the provider boundary is deliberately converted into an inspectable provider_error
Call budget is enforced before any dispatch — the hard_gates node computes traces × judges and raises if it exceeds max_calls (test_call_budget_fails_before_dispatch)

Human resolutions are bound to the SHA-256 hash of the dataset file bytes plus the run ID, so a resolution cannot be replayed against a mutated dataset; resolutions table has a composite FK into review_queue

The Ollama adapter rejects non-loopback and credential-bearing URLs in __post_init__ (hostname must be localhost/127.0.0.1/::1), with a parameterised test covering it; there is no paid-provider fallback path
HTML report escapes untrusted trace IDs via html.escape, with a dedicated regression test (test_report_escapes_untrusted_trace_id)

README and docs state the limits plainly: fixture judge scores are explicitly not evidence of LLM judge quality, cost is left unknown rather than estimated when Ollama does not report it, and the Dockerfile is marked as built-but-unverified
