repos.name: resumeproof
repos.tagline: Kills a workflow process between the side effect and its ack, then resumes and audits the result
repos.problem_solved: Agent workflows that call external tools have an unrecoverable window between committing a side effect and recording the acknowledgement. If the process dies there, a naive retry can double-charge and a naive failure can lose a completed effect. ResumeProof makes that window reproducible by actually killing a child process at that point, and shows which invariants survive idempotency and which force a human reconciliation.
repos.what_it_does: Runs a local agent-style workflow whose 'tool call' is a separate SQLite database acting as a merchant. The demo spawns child processes that call os._exit(86) immediately after the tool ledger commits but before the journal records the acknowledgement, then restarts the workflows in fresh processes. The idempotent path replays the original receipt on resume and ends with exactly one effect; the non-idempotent path detects that a prior process died mid-call, marks the workflow unknown, and refuses to retry — it can only be closed by an explicit audited reconcile command. Approvals store the SHA-256 digest of canonical action JSON, so editing an unstarted action changes the digest and pushes the workflow back to pending_approval. Every state transition is appended to an events timeline.
repos.architecture: src/ layout with a thin WorkflowEngine over two stores: a Journal (workflows + events tables) and a ToolLedger simulating a cooperating external tool. State transitions all run inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions, and claim/tool-call/acknowledge is wrapped in a cross-process OS file lock (msvcrt.locking on Windows, fcntl.flock on POSIX) so a crash releases it. Zero runtime dependencies — the whole thing is stdlib.
highlights: The crash is real, not mocked: the engine calls os._exit(86) after the ledger commits, and the demo spawns actual child processes so resume happens in a genuinely new interpreter

Idempotency is enforced in the ledger schema, not in application code — a partial unique index (one_effect_per_key ON effects(idempotency_key)) makes a duplicate effect impossible at the database level
The non-idempotent path deliberately refuses to be clever: a recovered attempt in non_idempotent mode is marked unknown and raises ReconciliationRequired rather than retrying

Approval is bound to the SHA-256 digest of canonical action JSON, and resume compares approval_digest to action_digest — a stale approval blocks execution (test_approval_is_bound_to_canonical_action_digest, test_action_cannot_change_after_execution_starts)
Corrupt, missing or action-mismatched receipts are handled as an explicit CorruptReceipt path into reconciliation instead of being treated as success
Cross-process locking plus BEGIN IMMEDIATE means concurrent resumptions share one durable attempt count, covered by test_concurrent_resumes_claim_one_attempt_and_one_effect
README states the negative results explicitly: this is not exactly-once delivery, one-machine SQLite is not a distributed transaction, and OS crash durability depends on filesystem settings
engineering_signals: 14 test functions in tests/test_workflow.py, each named after an invariant (crash-resume non-duplication, idempotency-key reuse rejection, retry cap durability, terminal-state protection, CLI JSON output)

repos.name: centaurloop-agent-governor
repos.tagline: Three small Python guards for agent patches: ast.parse check, banned-phrase scan, log truncation
repos.problem_solved: Aims to stop autonomous coding agents from committing hallucinated or placeholder code by validating a proposed patch before it reaches the workspace, and to keep agent loop telemetry from flooding the prompt context window.
repos.what_it_does: A single 3.4 KB module (src/governor.py) with three independent classes. ASTGate wraps ast.parse and returns (ok, message), formatting SyntaxError line/column into a diagnostic string. NegativeConstraintEnforcer does a substring scan for banned phrases, defaulting to TODO, TBD, INSERT LINK and example.com. ContextCompactor truncates a log to the last N lines, prepending a count of omitted lines and re-attaching up to three lines matching ERROR / Exception / Traceback / Fail. That is the entire implementation — the classes are standalone helpers with no orchestrator, no CLI and no integration between them.
repos.architecture: One flat module, src/governor.py, exposing three unconnected classes with no shared pipeline object. tests/test_governor.py imports them directly. No package metadata (no pyproject.toml or setup.py), so it is not installable — tests rely on rootdir imports.

ContextCompactor's tail-plus-error-lines strategy preserves error signal while bounding size, and reports the number of omitted lines so the truncation is visible to the reader
NegativeConstraintEnforcer takes the banned list as a constructor parameter, so the default placeholder set can be replaced with a project-specific one

repos.name: kindrelay
repos.tagline: Local-first React app turning volunteer handover notes into cited, human-reviewed task exports
repos.problem_solved: When a volunteer leaves a role, the knowledge of what still needs doing lives in unstructured notes. KindRelay converts those notes into discrete tasks that carry a citation back to the exact source line, requires a human to approve each one, and only then lets them be exported to a successor.
repos.what_it_does: A browser-only workspace that stores sources, tasks and review history in IndexedDB. Draft task suggestions are extracted deterministically: `src/suggestions/deterministic.ts` matches only the line prefixes `ACTION:`, `TODO:` and `- [ ]`, and the remainder of the line becomes both the task title and its verbatim citation quote — no owner, date or completion is ever inferred. Every suggestion stays a draft until a human approves it, and only approved, selected tasks can be exported as JSON or escaped Markdown. Sources and citation excerpts are SHA-256 hashed (WebCrypto `crypto.subtle.digest`) so packets can be checked for corruption on import; imported packets always land in a new workspace with tasks reset to draft.
repos.architecture: Vite + React 19 SPA with clearly separated layers under src/: `domain/` (types, validation, mutations, gap analysis, hashing), `storage/` (a ~20KB IndexedDB repository plus a transaction wrapper and its own input-validation layer), `import-export/` (packet codec, JSON schema, Markdown renderer), `suggestions/` (the deterministic extractor), and `ui/` (six React components). No backend, no accounts, no network calls.
highlights: The suggestion engine is deliberately non-AI: a 30-line pure function over three literal line prefixes, so every draft is traceable to an exact source line and revision (src/suggestions/deterministic.ts)

tests/import-export/security.test.ts (19.8KB) runs a one-at-a-time corruption matrix against real export output — unknown root/nested fields, a `__proto__` prototype-pollution key, duplicate tasks and sources, a dangling source reference, invalid revision/date/state enums, wrong schema version, an uppercased digest, and a tampered excerpt — asserting each is rejected on import

repos.name: transactional-outbox-engine
repos.tagline: In-memory Python model of the transactional outbox pattern with idempotent consumer dedup
repos.problem_solved: Illustrates the dual-write problem: when a service must both persist domain state and emit an event, doing so against two systems can leave them inconsistent. The outbox pattern writes both to one store, then relays events asynchronously with deduplication on the consumer side.
repos.what_it_does: A single 2.2 KB Python module (src/outbox.py) modelling four collaborators: OutboxEvent (uuid + PENDING status + timestamp), MockDB (two in-memory dicts/lists standing in for an orders table and an outbox table), TransactionalOutbox (writes order + event through one MockDB call), EventRelayer (drains PENDING events and flips them to PUBLISHED), and IdempotentConsumer (dict keyed on event_id; returns False on a replay). Three pytest tests cover the atomic write, the relayer drain, and duplicate suppression, and they pass in GitHub Actions. There is no database, no broker client, and no CDC: MockDB.save_order_atomic is two collection mutations with a comment claiming atomicity, and nothing in the repo imports or talks to Kafka or RabbitMQ despite the README and repo topics.
repos.architecture: Flat single-package layout: src/outbox.py holds all five classes, tests/test_outbox.py holds three tests, plus SPEC.md and USER_STORIES.md as separate design docs and one GitHub Actions workflow. Everything is in-process and synchronous; the 'asynchronous relayer' is a for-loop over pending events. Dependency direction is clean (TransactionalOutbox and EventRelayer both take a MockDB; the relayer takes a consumer as an argument), so a real DB or broker could be substituted, but no such adapter or interface is defined.
highlights: IdempotentConsumer.process returns a boolean rather than raising, so a replayed event_id is a normal control-flow outcome — the dedup test asserts both the False return and that the store still holds exactly one entry
Constructor injection throughout (TransactionalOutbox(db), EventRelayer(db), drain_and_publish(consumer)) leaves seams where a real datastore or broker adapter could be substituted
The design is written down before the code: USER_STORIES.md states the two behaviours as Gherkin scenarios, and each maps to a named test in tests/test_outbox.py
engineering_signals: tests/test_outbox.py — 3 real assertions-bearing tests (atomic write, relayer drain, duplicate suppression), not placeholders
.github/workflows/ci.yml — Actions workflow pinned to Python 3.12 running `pytest -v tests/` on push and PR to main/master
Latest CI run 'CI Test Suite' (id 33933447900) is green, so the suite genuinely passes
SPEC.md records three numbered ADRs and USER_STORIES.md states acceptance criteria as Gherkin scenarios
Conventional-commit messages (feat/test/docs/ci scopes) across all 8 commits
repos.caveats: Substantially oversold relative to what the code does. The repo description, topics (kafka, cdc) and README promise a 'CDC event relayer' that 'streams messages to Kafka/RabbitMQ' — no broker or CDC code exists anywhere in the repo; the persistence layer is a class literally named MockDB backed by a dict, and 'atomic' is a comment, not a transaction. SPEC.md asserts P99 < 1.5 ms and >= 95 % branch coverage; there is no benchmark and no coverage tooling in CI, so neither number is measurable from the repo. LICENSE is a 159-byte stub that cuts off mid-sentence at 'obtaining a copy...' — GitHub classifies it as 'other', not MIT, despite the MIT badge in the README. Scale and provenance: 2.2 KB of source, 8 commits all within ~3 hours on 2026-09-04/05, with duplicated commit messages repeated three times and bodies naming 'Dev Agent', 'QA Agent' and 'BA Agent' — this reads as autonomous-agent-generated scaffolding, not sustained work. Compiled __pycache__/*.pyc files are committed. 0 stars, 0 forks, untouched since creation. One real logic gap: EventRelayer.drain_and_publish discards the consumer's False return value, marking an event PUBLISHED and incrementing its count even when the consumer deduplicated it. Best presented as a teaching artefact or article companion (the README links a DEV.to write-up), never as a production engine.

repos.name: pulse-signals-engine
repos.tagline: Python signals runtime: auto dependency tracking, lazy computed caching, batched effects
repos.problem_solved: Models the core of a fine-grained reactivity system — the kind that underpins Angular signals, SolidJS or Vue refs — where reading a value inside a derivation automatically records the dependency, and a write invalidates only the nodes that actually depend on it rather than re-checking a whole component tree.
repos.what_it_does: A 3.5 KB Python module (src/signals.py) implementing a reactive graph from scratch: a module-global _current_consumer acts as the tracking context, so Signal.get() registers whichever Computed or Effect is currently evaluating as a subscriber. Writes push dirty marks down the graph; Computed.get() pulls lazily, recomputing only when dirty and caching otherwise. Each re-evaluation first discards its old subscriber edges and rebuilds them, so conditional dependencies do not leak. A batch() context manager diverts effect re-runs into a pending set and flushes it once on exit. Five pytest tests cover signal get/set, computed caching, diamond-shaped dependency evaluation counts, batch coalescing, and a cycle-detection case; all pass in CI. Note the entire repo is Python — there is no Angular, TypeScript, DOM or zoneless-change-detection code anywhere, despite the name, description and topics.
repos.architecture: Node/Consumer base classes split the two roles: Node owns a subscriber set and notify_subscribers(); Consumer owns a dependency set and mark_dirty(). Signal is a Node, Effect is a Consumer, and Computed multiply-inherits both — which is what lets derived values sit in the middle of a graph. Invalidation is push (mark_dirty propagates, and Computed short-circuits propagation if already dirty), evaluation is pull (lazy, cached). Batching state lives in module-level globals (_in_batch, _pending_effects) rather than in an owner object.
highlights: Dependency edges are torn down and rebuilt on every evaluation (both Computed.get and Effect.run clear self.dependencies and discard themselves from each old node's subscribers) — the correct handling for branch-dependent reads, and the detail naive implementations usually miss
Computed.mark_dirty propagates only on the clean-to-dirty transition, so a single signal write does not fan out repeatedly through an already-invalidated subgraph

Lazy pull evaluation plus dirty caching means a diamond dependency (a to b and c, both to d) evaluates d once per read after an update rather than once per upstream path — the test asserts the exact evaluation count

The tracking context is saved and restored around each evaluation (prev = _current_consumer, restored in a finally block), so nested computed reads do not corrupt the enclosing consumer's dependency set
An _evaluating re-entrancy flag raises a typed CycleDependencyError instead of blowing the Python stack
engineering_signals: tests/test_signals.py — 5 tests with real assertions, including an evaluation-counter test that checks recomputation counts rather than only final values

Latest CI run 'CI Test Suite' (id 33933445127) is green
SPEC.md (three numbered ADRs) and USER_STORIES.md (Gherkin scenarios that map onto named tests) are committed alongside the code

repos.caveats: The framing does not match the artefact. Repo name, description and topics claim a zoneless reactive engine for Angular 19 in TypeScript, and the README claims 'locked 60fps under 50,000 events/sec' and 'O(1) change localization' — the repo is 100 % Python with no Angular, TypeScript, DOM or benchmark code, so none of those numbers is measurable here and the fps/throughput claims are unsupported. README claims '100% Test Coverage' and SPEC.md claims >= 95 % branch coverage and P99 < 1.5 ms; CI runs bare `pytest -v` with no coverage or timing tooling. test_cycle_detection is misnamed and does not test what it says: its 'recursive_fn' merely reads a signal and adds 1, no cycle is constructed, and the imported CycleDependencyError is never asserted — so the cycle-detection path is effectively untested. Batching state is module-global and non-reentrant: a nested batch() clears _in_batch on the inner exit, flushing early, and nothing is thread-safe. Provenance and scale: 3.5 KB of source, 10 commits all within ~3 hours on 2026-09-04/05 with messages repeated verbatim and bodies naming 'Dev Agent', 'QA Agent' and 'BA Agent' — agent-generated scaffolding rather than sustained development. LICENSE is a 159-byte fragment truncated at 'obtaining a copy...' (GitHub reads it as 'other', not MIT, contradicting the README badge), and __pycache__/*.pyc files are committed. 0 stars, 0 forks, no activity since creation. The signals core itself is the genuinely interesting part and holds up on its own; show it as a from-scratch reactivity implementation, and drop the Angular/60fps framing entirely.

repos.name: ebpf-credscan-security
repos.tagline: Userspace Python regex scanner for leaked API keys and prompt-injection strings in payloads
repos.problem_solved: Detecting credentials (OpenAI, AWS, GitHub tokens, PEM private keys) and prompt-injection strings in outbound payload bytes before they leave a service.
repos.what_it_does: Despite the eBPF framing in the name and README, the working code is a ~50-line pure-Python userspace scanner. `CredScanFirewall.inspect_packet(src_ip, dst_ip, payload: bytes)` runs six compiled regexes over the payload and returns `(PacketDecision.ALLOW|DROP, Optional[SecurityAlert])`, appending a `SecurityAlert` dataclass (timestamp, threat type, src/dst IP, 30-byte match snippet) to an in-memory audit list retrievable via `get_alerts()`. Patterns cover `sk-proj-`, `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}`, `ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}`, PEM PRIVATE KEY headers, and two case-insensitive literals (`IGNORE PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS`, `PRINT SYSTEM PROMPT`). The single C file, `src/credscan_sock.bpf.c` (386 bytes), is a stub: a `SEC("sockops")` function whose body is one comment and `return 0;`. Nothing loads, compiles, or attaches it, and no packet is ever intercepted at the kernel level.
repos.architecture: Flat: `src/scanner.py` (the entire implementation), `src/credscan_sock.bpf.c` (unbuilt stub), `tests/test_credscan.py`, plus SPEC.md and USER_STORIES.md. Pattern list is a module-private list of `(compiled_regex, threat_type)` tuples; detection is first-match-wins, so only one threat type is reported per payload. No loader, no build system, no packaging, no CLI.
highlights: Detection logic is genuinely readable and honest in shape: `inspect_packet` returns an explicit `(PacketDecision, Optional[SecurityAlert])` tuple rather than a bare bool, so callers get the reason alongside the verdict
Match snippets are truncated to 30 bytes and decoded with `errors='replace'` before being stored in an alert, which avoids echoing a full secret into the audit log
Threat taxonomy is typed as named constants (OPENAI_API_KEY_LEAK, AWS_CREDENTIAL_LEAK, PRIVATE_KEY_LEAK, PROMPT_INJECTION_OVERRIDE/EXFILTRATION) rather than free-text strings
The five pytest cases exercise real code paths — drop-on-token, drop-on-PEM-key, block-on-injection, allow-benign fast path, and audit-log accumulation — and the CI run for the current HEAD is green
engineering_signals: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — real GitHub Actions workflow, Python 3.12 on ubuntu-latest, runs `pytest -v tests/`; latest run on 2026-09-05 completed with conclusion `success`
`tests/test_credscan.py` — 5 pytest tests that import and call the actual `CredScanFirewall`, asserting both decisions and threat types (not placeholder assertions)
`SPEC.md` and `USER_STORIES.md` present, the latter written as Gherkin Given/When/Then scenarios mapped to the three README features

The headline claim — kernel-level eBPF interception of outbound TCP socket buffers — is not implemented: `src/credscan_sock.bpf.c` is a 386-byte stub that unconditionally returns 0, there is no Makefile, clang/bpftool step, libbpf or BCC loader, and CI never compiles it. Everything that works is userspace Python regex over a bytes argument the caller supplies; nothing touches a socket, a packet, or the kernel. repos.name: concurrent-cache-dotnet9
repos.tagline: Lock-based LRU+TTL cache in Python with a compare-and-swap API, plus a small C# sketch
repos.problem_solved: An in-process key/value cache with LRU eviction, TTL expiry, hit/miss/eviction statistics, and an atomic compare-and-swap update path for contended keys.
repos.what_it_does: The functioning implementation is `src/cache.py`: `ConcurrentMemoryCache` backed by an `OrderedDict` under a single `threading.Lock`. `get` handles TTL expiry inline (deleting the expired entry and counting it as both a miss and an eviction) and does an LRU touch via `move_to_end`; `set` bumps a per-entry `version` on overwrite and evicts oldest-first with `popitem(last=False)` until under capacity; `compare_and_swap(key, expected, new_val)` swaps only if the current value matches, returning bool. `CacheEntry` uses `__slots__`, and `get_stats()` returns a `CacheStats` dataclass. The separate `src/ConcurrentCache.cs` (1109 bytes) is a sketch, not the product: `ZeroAllocCache` wraps `MemoryPool<byte>.Shared` and a `ConcurrentDictionary<string, IMemoryOwner<byte>>` with `Set`/`TryGet`/`Dispose`. It has no project file, is never compiled, and its declared `_evictionChannel` (`Channel.CreateBounded<string>(10000)`) is never written to or read from.
repos.architecture: Two parallel, unconnected implementations. Python side: single-lock `OrderedDict` LRU with lazy TTL checks on read and eager capacity eviction on write; counters kept as plain ints inside the lock. C# side: one standalone file with no .csproj, .sln, or test project. `tests/` targets only the Python. SPEC.md and USER_STORIES.md describe the intended design (bounded-channel background eviction, Span<T> slicing) rather than what is built.
highlights: `compare_and_swap` gives the cache a real read-modify-write primitive, and the test drives it properly — 5 threads x 100 retry-loop increments asserting an exact final value of 500, which is a genuine race-condition test rather than a smoke check
TTL expiry is handled lazily on read rather than by a sweeper thread, so an expired key is deleted and counted on the access that finds it — a reasonable choice for a single-process cache
Per-entry `version` counter incremented on every mutation, which is the right foundation for optimistic concurrency
`CacheEntry` uses `__slots__` to cut per-entry dict overhead, a deliberate memory choice consistent with the repo's stated intent
Eviction, TTL, LRU touch and stats are all covered by tests that assert observable state (`stats.size <= 10`, `stats.evictions >= 5`, post-sleep miss)
engineering_signals: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — GitHub Actions running `pytest -v tests/` on Python 3.12 / ubuntu-latest; latest run 2026-09-05 concluded `success`
`tests/test_concurrent_cache.py` — 5 tests against the real class, including a genuine multithreaded CAS contention test and a TTL-expiry test with a real sleep
`SPEC.md` and `USER_STORIES.md` with Gherkin scenarios covering the three claimed features
repos.caveats: The claims and the code diverge badly. The repo is titled a lock-free .NET 9 engine, but the only working code is Python guarded by a single `threading.Lock` — every operation, including `compare_and_swap`, takes that lock, so it is lock-based by construction, and the CAS is a mutex-protected swap rather than an atomic primitive. The README's '850k req/s', '500,000 requests/sec' and 'zero Gen0 allocations' are supported by nothing in the repo: there is no benchmark, no BenchmarkDotNet, no allocation measurement; the closest thing is a test asserting 4000 Python dict operations finish in under 1 second. The C# file is decorative — no .csproj or .sln, so nothing compiles it and CI never touches it — and it contains real defects if it ever were used: `Set` overwrites `_store[key]` without disposing the previously rented `IMemoryOwner<byte>`, leaking pooled buffers on every overwrite, and `TryGet` returns the whole rented `owner.Memory`, which `MemoryPool.Rent` may size larger than the data written, so callers get trailing garbage past the real payload length. The advertised background `BoundedChannel<T>` eviction exists only as an unused field. The README's own 'Running Tests' section says `pytest` in a repo named for .NET 9. Provenance is visible: 6 commits all on 2026-09-05, messages naming 'BA Agent', 'QA Agent' and 'Dev Agent', with the Dev/QA commit pair duplicated as if a generation run was repeated; the three SPEC.md ADRs are boilerplate identical to those in ebpf-credscan-security. `__pycache__` is committed. The LICENSE is truncated at 159 bytes ('...obtaining a copy...'), so GitHub reports the licence as 'other' despite the MIT badge. 0 stars, 0 forks, single `master` branch.

merged.title: fix(proxy): invalidate end-user spend counter and cache on budget reset (#39726)
merged.what_it_fixed: An end-user budget reset zeroed the spend in Postgres but not the cached spend counter, so multi-worker and multi-replica proxy deployments kept returning HTTP 429 'Budget has been exceeded' after the budget window had already rolled over, until the caches expired on their own; the fix zeroes spend:end_user:<id> in both in-memory and Redis caches, evicts the cached end-user object on every worker rather than just the one running the reset job, extends rollover carry to default end-user budgets as well as explicit ones, and floors a stale cached spend against LiteLLM_EndUserTable.spend with a 5-second in-process cache, across 283 added lines with three dedicated regression-test files (+283/-30, 6 files).

merged.title: fix(lsp): overlap auxiliary LSP warmup with primary server during resync (#2540)
merged.what_it_fixed: On a cold first edit the auxiliary LSP servers (opengrep, ast-grep) were only spawned after the primary server's resync had been awaited, so the edit hook paid primary spawn plus auxiliary spawn strictly in sequence (~7s observed); the fix kicks off getAuxiliaryClientsForFile unawaited at resync time under the turn's ambient abort signal so the two spawns overlap and the later with-auxiliary request either finds them warm or joins the same in-flight acquisition, adds optional maxWaitMs/signal/hook bounding per server, and records a new auxiliary_readiness latency phase excluded from stall attribution (+349/-5, 9 files, including a 227-line new concurrency test).

merged.title: fix(config-write): skip redundant .gitignore append when existing rule covers path (#1484)
merged.what_it_fixed: ensure_gitignored only checked for an exact line match when writing local-scope files such as .claude/settings.local.json, so when an ancestor rule like /.claude, .claude/ or .claude already ignored the whole directory it still appended duplicate entries and left unexpected working-tree modifications on main; the fix adds _is_gitignored_by_existing_rules to match root-anchored directory rules, unanchored directory rules, exact lines with or without a leading slash, and basename wildcards such as *.bak, turning already-covered paths into a clean no-op (+261/-9, 3 files, 155 lines of it tests).

merged.title: test: extract shared vitest base config to de-duplicate n8n-workflow alias (#7)
merged.what_it_fixed: The CJS fixture node requires n8n-workflow while the ESM test suites import the ESM build, producing two copies of the same classes and breaking instanceof checks; the alias pinning resolution to CJS had been copy-pasted into six separate package vitest configs, so the fix extracts a root vitest.config.base.ts holding that alias once and has every package extend it through mergeConfig while keeping its own coverage and environment settings (+109/-84 across 7 files, a net reduction in duplicated config).

merged.title: fix(postprocess): attach unmatched chaptered audio files to existing book group (#1176)
merged.what_it_fixed: Downloading an audiobook with 250+ chaptered tracks produced two split book folders, because indexer XML capped the release file list at roughly 110 entries, match_plan_to_files matched only those to the planned book, and the remaining 140+ files fell through to heuristic grouping which parsed the folder name and invented a second book; the fix checks unmatched files before that fallback and appends chaptered audio (.flac, .mp3, .aac) to an existing group when it shares the directory or the plan was single-book, while leaving standalone .m4b/.epub files and separate subfolders on the old path (+97/-2, 2 files, 76 lines of tests covering truncated lists, CD1/CD2 multi-disc, and multi-book packs).

merged.title: refactor(json): rename json_dump to json_dumps (#1399)
merged.what_it_fixed: Not a bug fix but an API-naming correction: the library's string-serialization helper was named json_dump, which in stdlib convention means writing to a file object rather than returning a string, so it was renamed to json_dumps in dmr.internal.json and dmr.openapi.dump with call sites in OpenAPIJsonView and the test client updated, a deprecated json_dump = json_dumps alias retained for backwards compatibility, tests added, and the breaking change recorded in CHANGELOG under 0.15.0 (+13/-9, 5 files).

merged.title: docs(skills): state negative boundaries in frontmatter descriptions (#284)
merged.what_it_fixed: Six Claude Code skills across two plugin packs had frontmatter descriptions that said what the skill covers but never what it excludes, so overlapping skills competed for the same prompts; the fix adds an explicit negative-boundary clause to each description naming the sibling skill that should handle the excluded case (for example, routing symbol searches away from graphify to code-search, and tool-schema questions away from auditing-agent-architecture to designing-tools-and-mcp), and bumps both packs 1.1.0 to 1.1.1 (+8/-8 across 8 files - one line changed per file).

merged.title: docs(policies): point docs at docs/policies/ and document trajectory_hint exception (#68)
merged.what_it_fixed: A four-line docstring correction: the policies package pointed readers at a tokenops-lld/policies/ directory that does not exist in the repository (now docs/policies/) and gave no reason why trajectory_hint is absent from the exported policy templates, which the change explains - it requires a Store and is configured in control/config.py instead (+4/-1, 1 file).

themes: Stale cache and cross-process state invalidation - the strongest theme and the one with the best evidence. The LiteLLM fix is a textbook distributed-cache coherence bug: authoritative DB state was reset but the derived counters on other workers and replicas were not, so enforcement kept using pre-reset values until TTL expiry.

Cold-start latency and accidental serialization - work that was independent was being awaited in sequence. The pi-lens LSP fix overlaps two spawns that had no dependency, cutting a ~7s edit-hook stall, and does it with proper abort-signal and deadline bounding rather than fire-and-forget.

Edge cases in matching and grouping logic where upstream data is incomplete or non-canonical - shelfmark's truncated indexer file lists producing phantom split albums, and clauster's .gitignore checker that only understood exact string matches and not the several equivalent forms a covering rule can take. Both are 'the happy path was implemented, the degraded-input path was not' bugs.

Build, test and CI configuration hygiene - de-duplicating a module-resolution alias across six package configs to keep instanceof working across a CJS/ESM boundary (n8n-probe), and clearing a schema-version drift warning (MiniSearch).
API naming consistency and deprecation-safe renames - json_dump to json_dumps with a retained alias, changelog entry and tests (django-modern-rest).

Documentation and metadata accuracy - correcting a docstring that pointed at a nonexistent directory (tokenops) and adding negative-boundary clauses to skill descriptions so a router stops mis-selecting overlapping skills (swarmery).

Across the unmerged work, a further theme is security-adjacent input validation: case-insensitive Host/Origin comparison, preserving non-canonical JSON-RPC numeric request IDs, rejecting null bytes in task IDs, and bounding string truncation against sentinel overflow. contributions.honest_framing:
Lead with 9, never 55. The number that survives a click-through is the merged count, because the exact GitHub search that produced this dataset is one URL any reviewer can reconstruct in ten seconds (is:pr author:amasen02 -user:amasen02), and it renders the merged/open/closed badges next to every row. A claim of "55 contributions" fails on first contact, and worse, it fails in a way that reframes everything else as inflation.

What to lead with, concretely: one merged fix in LiteLLM, a 58k-star LLM gateway used in production, resolving a distributed cache-invalidation bug where end-user budget resets left stale spend counters on other workers and replicas and kept returning HTTP 429 after the window rolled over. That single PR is the strongest asset in this record - 283 lines with three dedicated regression-test files, a documented two-replica/two-worker reproduction rig, and a real merge by a project with a CLA and an automated review gate. Then say "plus eight further merged PRs in smaller projects" and let the reader open them. Two of those eight are a one-line schema URL bump and a four-line docstring correction; do not describe them individually or they will be found and counted against the rest. The three worth naming after LiteLLM are pi-lens (concurrency, 227-line new test), clauster (gitignore rule coverage, 155 test lines), and shelfmark (audiobook grouping, 76 test lines) - those three plus LiteLLM are the four that show engineering judgment rather than housekeeping.

Be explicit about project reach rather than letting the reader discover it. Only one merge is in a project above 10k stars. Four of the nine are in repos with under 100 stars, three of those under 5. If the portfolio implies "merged into major open source" without that qualifier, the qualifier is what the reviewer will remember finding on their own. Say it first: "one merge in a major project, eight in smaller ones."

Open PRs: describe as submitted and pending review, with the submission date attached, and never under a heading that says "contributions". "32 pull requests submitted, awaiting maintainer review (most opened 3-6 September 2026)" is accurate; "contributions to AutoGPT, CrewAI, Milvus and LangGraph" is not, because those PRs have zero reviews and are days old. An unreviewed PR is a submission, not a contribution - the distinction is the whole difference between a record that holds up and one that does not. Also note honestly that at analysis time exactly one open PR carried an approval (a 1-star repo) and two carried CHANGES_REQUESTED. If the portfolio is dated, this section will age badly in both directions; timestamp it or refresh it before sending.

Closed-unmerged: leave all 14 out of the portfolio, but do not assume they are invisible. They are on the public profile and three of them carry maintainer language that is materially damaging if a reviewer reads it cold. pallets/jinja #2264 was publicly retitled "[rejected AI]" by a maintainer - the rejection is in the title string itself, so it is legible from the search results page without opening anything. twisted/twisted #12838 was closed by glyph after he wrote that the contributor's comments read like LLM output, asked to schedule a video call to confirm a human was involved, and concluded the code had "a truly unreasonable amount of duplication". classroomio #1050 was closed with "this is AI slop. You said you added a video but no video". That last one is the most serious, because it is not a dispute about tooling - it is a maintainer saying a claim in a PR comment was not true. That is a credibility finding, not a style disagreement, and no framing repairs it; the only response is to be able to account for it directly if asked.

The remaining eleven closures are genuinely defensible and can be mentioned if a conversation goes there: three were auto-closed by policy bots for not being assigned to the linked issue (LangGraph, both MCP Python SDK PRs) with no human ever reviewing the code; four were withdrawn by the author, including one superseded by an upstream fix; and four were overtaken - notably fastdocparse #59, where the maintainer called the implementation "solid" and the loss "pure timing, not a quality call", which is the one closed PR that reads as a positive if quoted. Starlette #3505 was closed on a measured 23.54% performance regression, which is a legitimate technical rejection and should be owned as one.

Two things to remove from the count entirely before publishing any number. atmoz-tech-challenge/ama-bandara #2 is a 2024 take-home interview exercise in a repo named after the candidate - it is not open-source contribution and including it in an OSS total is the kind of padding that invalidates the rest. And decide deliberately whether paperclipai/paperclip #9757 belongs here at all; it may be work-adjacent rather than volunteer open source, and mixing the two categories invites a question you do not want to answer defensively.

On AI assistance, the honest position is disclosure, and the reason is tactical as much as ethical: at least three maintainers have already said in public, in writing, on this profile, that they believe the work was AI-generated. The reviewer will encounter their assessment before they encounter any denial. Saying plainly that these were AI-assisted and describing what the human contribution was - issue selection, reproduction rigs, test design, iterating through review - is a defensible and increasingly ordinary claim in 2026. It also explains the shape of the data that otherwise looks worst: 51 PRs in four days across 40 unrelated repositories is not a pattern any reviewer will read as organic, and offering no explanation for it invites the least charitable one.

The framing that survives scrutiny, in one line: "9 merged open-source PRs, including a distributed cache-invalidation fix in LiteLLM (58k stars); 32 more submitted and pending review." Everything true, nothing that breaks on a click, and the strongest single piece of work in the first clause.

synthesis.summary: Ama Senevirathne (GitHub: amasen02) builds backend systems, developer CLIs and agent tooling across C#/.NET, TypeScript and Node. The through-line in the public code is that correctness claims get turned into checks a reader can run: a twelve-service .NET 10 platform pins each concurrency guarantee with an N-way test against a real database engine in a container — twenty-five parallel invoice allocators asserting the result set is exactly {1..25}, unique and gap-free; a segmented HTTP downloader proves its lock-free parallel assembly by asserting that segmented and single-stream output are SHA-256-identical; an agent pipeline decodes its own delivered GIF and checks frame delays, loop-seam hashes and static-region flicker rather than trusting the encoder. The same instinct runs through the security-shaped code — a fetcher that resolves DNS itself and pins the resolved address into the request's lookup callback so a rebind between check and connect cannot occur; an Angular front end that carries a session cookie into SignalR so no bearer token ever exists in JavaScript. One merged fix in BerriAI/litellm, a 58k-star LLM gateway, cleared stale end-user spend counters that kept returning HTTP 429 after a budget window had already rolled over.

groupings.blurb: State that has to stay consistent across workers, replicas and storage engines, with the race made falsifiable. In FreshCart: an outbox drained by claim-by-update with a crash-recovering lease so two publisher replicas claim disjoint sets with no distributed lock; a one-payment-per-order invariant enforced by a partial unique index in the Mongo event store rather than in an asynchronously projected read model; an idempotency row written inside the same MySQL transaction as the additive upserts so a redelivery cannot double-count lifetime value. In litellm: the same class of bug from the other side — authoritative state was reset in Postgres but the derived counters on other workers were not, so enforcement kept using pre-reset values until TTL expiry.

groupings.theme: Systems-level developer CLIs, where the real work is data integrity
groupings.blurb: Single-purpose tools whose interesting decisions are all about not corrupting or losing the user's bytes: a resume sidecar that is only trusted when size, chunk size and ETag/Last-Modified all still match, written by atomic temp-file rename so a reader never sees a half-written bitmap; hardlink replacement done as link-to-temp-then-rename so an interrupted operation cannot destroy the original; failure contained at file granularity so one unreadable directory does not throw away an hour-long scan. Feature one dedupe tool here, not two.

groupings.theme: Agent reliability — refusing to take a model's word for anything
groupings.blurb: A pipeline built around the assumption that the model is the least trustworthy component. Every quoted fact must be found verbatim (after NFKC and punctuation normalisation) in the actually-fetched extract, with the match offset and a SHA-256 of that extract recorded. Every text slot the diagram will render must be covered by a claim citing a fact ID or the literal token 'authoring', and a classifier escalates anything containing a number, a percentage or an absolute like 'only' or 'guarantees'. Layout defects are found by measuring the real render in Chromium via getBBox() and repaired deterministically, so a layout problem never costs a model call. The delivered GIF is then decoded and checked frame by frame. Where the pipeline cannot measure something it says so: a critic running without vision records readability as 'unmeasured', not 'pass'.

Zoneless Angular 20 on signal stores, where authentication never touches JavaScript: the SignalR hub is built with withCredentials and deliberately no accessTokenFactory, so no bearer token lands in a query string or in memory for XSS to lift — and the repo pays the resulting same-origin cost in its dev proxy, nginx config and ingress. Realtime-primary with a bounded poll fallback whose interval and attempt cap are injection tokens rather than a hard-coded setInterval, and hub lifecycle transitions serialised through a promise chain so auth flapping cannot leak duplicate handlers.

One DI-registered interface over five LLM providers, where the README's invariant — every failure of this SDK is a PolyAIException — is enforced structurally rather than documented: a single malformed-response boundary takes each provider's parse function as a delegate and runs it inside the try, and the catch filter is deliberately narrowed to three exception types with a comment stating that anything else is an SDK defect and must keep escaping. Four providers × three malformed payload shapes are driven through it in tests.

headline_details.detail: InvoiceRepositoryTests fires 25 parallel allocators at a Testcontainers MySQL 8.0 and asserts the returned set is exactly {1..25} — unique and gap-free — which proves the invoice-number allocation is a single atomic statement and not a read-then-write. One file, real database engine, falsifiable in about a minute. Card line: 'Gap-free invoice numbering under 25-way concurrency, proven against a real MySQL container — not asserted in a README.' (Runner-up if a different flavour is wanted: the payment event store enforces one-payment-per-order with a partial unique index on OrderId filtered to Version == 1, so a duplicate initiate fails at the source of truth instead of in an asynchronously projected SQL table.)

Resetting an end-user budget zeroed spend in Postgres but left the derived counters on every other worker and replica intact, so a 58k-star LLM gateway kept returning HTTP 429 'Budget has been exceeded' after the window had already rolled over, until caches expired on their own. The fix zeroes spend:end_user:<id> in both in-memory and Redis caches, evicts the cached end-user object on every worker rather than only the one running the reset job, and floors a stale cached spend against the authoritative table row behind a 5-second in-process cache. +283/−30 across 6 files with three dedicated regression-test files, merged 5 September 2026. Link straight to the diff.

Grounding is enforced mechanically, not by prompt: every quote in the fact sheet must survive NFKC, punctuation and whitespace normalisation and then be found as a substring of the extract that was actually fetched (minimum 12 characters / 4 words), with the match offset and a SHA-256 of the extract recorded; a fact sheet whose source metadata disagrees with what the collector retrieved is rejected outright. Card line: 'The model cannot assert anything the pipeline did not fetch — and the delivered GIF is decoded and checked frame by frame before it is called done.'

It refuses to segment a download unless the server proves it honours ranges: the probe sends Range: 0-0 and accepts segmentation only when the reply is 206 with Content-Range exactly {from 0, to 0}, because a server that returns 206 while ignoring the header produces a file that is corrupt but 'successful'. Auto-decompression is switched off with an explicit Accept-Encoding: identity for the same reason — it corrupts byte-range arithmetic. The payoff is in the tests: segmented and single-stream output of the same payload are asserted SHA-256-identical, which is a real proof that the lock-free write-to-offset assembly is correct rather than merely non-crashing.

A duplicate group is a group of physical files, not paths: files are collapsed by device+inode before any hashing, so reclaimable space is size × (physicalFiles − 1) — provably what a cleanup actually frees — and a second --hardlink pass finds nothing to do. Picking the right domain type removed an entire class of accounting bugs instead of patching them, and two tests assert exactly that. The destructive path is link-to-temp-then-atomic-rename, never unlink-then-link, pinned by a test that points the kept path at a nonexistent file and asserts the original survives untouched.

The SSE reader is written as a while(true) loop over ReadLineAsync and deliberately never touches StreamReader.EndOfStream, with the reason in the code: EndOfStream refills the buffer with a synchronous, non-cancellable read, so on an open-but-idle connection the loop condition parks and the CancellationToken is never observed. That is a genuinely non-obvious cancellation bug that most hand-rolled streaming clients ship with, and this one is documented at the call site.

The SignalR connection is built with withCredentials: true and no accessTokenFactory at all — a comment in the code says so explicitly. The usual SPA pattern puts a bearer token in a hub query string (where it lands in logs and referrers) or in JS memory (where XSS can lift it); pushing the session cookie through the gateway's cookie-to-JWT exchange removes both paths, and the repo pays the strict same-origin cost it creates in proxy.conf.json, nginx.conf and the ingress.
